items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Okanagan Nation Alliance Restores Salmon Access to Okanagan Lake Reading Time: 3 minutes The Okanagan Nation Alliance is restoring salmon access to Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years through a newly completed dam fish passage. The Okanagan Nation Alliance has reconnected sockeye salmon to Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly a century. A new fish passage now lets fish bypass a dam that has blocked the route since 1953. The milestone caps decades of restoration work led by Syilx Okanagan communities in British Columbia. Dams and channel work built through the last century cut salmon off from more than 350 square kilometers of lake habitat. The Okanagan Lake Dam at Penticton became one of the last major barriers standing in the salmon’s path. Until now, fish had no permanent route to swim safely around it. The Okanagan Nation Alliance runs one of Canada’s most extensive Indigenous-led fisheries programs. It comprises eight member communities and manages hatcheries, habitat restoration, and dam modifications across the Okanagan Basin. Its fisheries team has spent more than two decades working to bring salmon back. For Syilx Okanagan communities, the reconnection means more than fish counts. Elders describe a longstanding relationship between their people and salmon, one rooted in responsibility rather than simple resource use. Opening ceremonies for the passage included songs and drumming, along with tributes to community leaders who pushed for its construction over many years. Engineers designed the completed passage as a nature-like channel rather than a traditional metal fish ladder. Grating along the top lets sunlight reach the water and allows visitors to watch fish pass underneath. The Okanagan Nation Alliance’s completed fish passage is designed as a natural-looking channel rather than a traditional metal fish ladder, with grating along the top that lets sunlight reach the water and lets visitors watch fish pass underneath. Photo courtesy of Okanagan Nation Alliance . The route gives steelhead, rainbow trout, sockeye, chinook, and kokanee access to the lake and 13 tributary streams. An adjustable barrier built into the design filters out invasive species trying to follow the same path. That balance lets native fish through while keeping unwanted species out. Salmon runs in the Okanagan once numbered in the hundreds of thousands before dam construction and river channelization fragmented their habitat. The Okanagan Lake Dam, built in 1953, included an earlier fishway that never worked well. Water levels made it unusable for salmon during much of the year. The passage builds on a broader restoration effort the Okanagan Nation Alliance has carried out since the 1990s. That work includes a 12-year sockeye reintroduction program in nearby Skaha Lake and roughly 50 habitat projects across the basin. Modifications to two other dams further downstream have also opened additional spawning grounds. A conservation hatchery run by the Alliance raises sockeye fry each spring for release into historical spawning areas. Students take part in some releases through a program that introduces them to salmon biology and Syilx culture. In 2026 alone, organizers released 330,000 sockeye fry across the territory. Recovering salmon runs have also revived a small commercial and community fishery on Osoyoos Lake. In recent years, the Okanagan Nation Alliance’s fishing crew has landed record numbers of returning sockeye there, with thousands of fish distributed to member communities for ceremonies, trade, and food. A stronger run into Okanagan Lake could extend that momentum further north. Okanagan sockeye form part of a larger population that migrates through the Columbia River Basin shared by Canada and the United States. According to the International Joint Commission, Okanagan-origin fish account for the largest share of sockeye returning to that binational system most years. That transboundary status makes the newly reopened habitat significant well beyond British Columbia. International reviewers have noted the project’s design. The passage was nominated for the International Fish Passage Project of Distinction and presented at a fish passage conference in California in 2026. Recognition like this signals growing interest in Indigenous-led approaches to river restoration. Returns to the reopened habitat are expected to stay modest at first, since warm river conditions have limited recent salmon numbers. Even so, the passage will remain open for every future migration season. For a Nation that has worked for generations to see salmon return, a permanent route into Okanagan Lake marks a turning point rather than an ending. The post The Okanagan Nation Alliance Restores Salmon Access to Okanagan Lake appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Μέσω πραγματικών γονέων, προπονητών γονέων, επιρροών και ειδικών, η σειρά φέρνει ειλικρινείς, διαφορετικές και σχετικές προοπτικές για το q…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. When Kiara Powar was 13, she came home from a badminton match, hugged her mother, and cried for an entire day. After years of playing the sport she loved, she had to give it up because severe migraines were causing blackouts on the court. For Shweta Powar, watching her daughter navigate the loss was heartbreaking. Kiara had already faced a lifelong health condition, bullying, and rejection from people she had grown up with. Now, she was being forced to step away from something that had brought her happiness. "I told her, 'It's okay if people talk about you. This is exactly when we have to fight back and keep working harder to prove our point,'" Shweta recalls. Today, Kiara is a sports presenter and sportscaster, hosting digital shows such as Bat, Ball Aur Baatein and Sports & The City . Her journey from a young badminton player to a career in sports has been shaped by the challenges she faced growing up with Type 1 diabetes, and the support of her parents, who never wanted her condition to limit her ambitions. With the support of her parents, doctors and coaches, Kiara trained professionally in badminton from the age of nine. For Shweta and her husband, Kiran Powar, a former first-class cricketer, the journey began when Kiara was just two years old and was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. The diagnosis meant learning to manage a condition they knew very little about. But as parents, they made one decision early on: they would help their daughter understand her condition without letting it dictate what she could aspire to. Learning to live with diabetes, one day at a time The signs began about a month before Kiara's diagnosis. She was urinating frequently and gradually losing her appetite. After initial consultations failed to identify the problem, her parents sought another medical opinion. Shweta encouraged Kiara to face setbacks with confidence rather than let other people's opinions hold her back. The doctor recognised the seriousness of her condition and asked them to rush her to a hospital. Kiara was admitted to the ICU, where she remained under observation for 48 hours before doctors confirmed that she had Type 1 diabetes. "We had heard the word diabetes, but we didn't know what Type 1 juvenile diabetes was or what had to be done," Shweta says. At the time, managing the condition meant four insulin injections a day. Shweta and Kiran had to learn how to administer the injections, monitor Kiara's sugar levels, and adjust insulin doses in consultation with her medical team. The first few months were especially difficult. Shweta remembers being afraid of giving her daughter the injections, while the family struggled with the social stigma surrounding the condition. Initially, they avoided family gatherings and social occasions, worried about people's reactions. But after six months, they realised that shielding Kiara from the world was not the answer. "We didn't want our child to grow up under fear. We wanted her to face it, challenge herself and fight against the odds," Shweta says. They began focusing on helping her live as normally as possible. Her school nurse helped with insulin injections during the day, while Shweta managed her morning routine and made sure she received her evening dose and meals on time. At home, the family followed the same food habits as Kiara, with homemade, sugar-free alternatives to sweets. The aim was not to make her feel different, but to help her understand what her body needed. When badminton became her refuge Growing up in a sporting family, Kiara developed an interest in tennis at seven and began playing badminton professionally at nine. She wanted to build a future connected to sports. Her parents supported her ambitions while working with her doctors, coaches, nutritionist and trainer to manage her health alongside training. She followed a disciplined routine, carried meals to practice, and had support available in case her sugar levels dropped. But adolescence brought challenges beyond diabetes. At 13, Kiara experienced severe emotional distress after relatives and cousins stopped communicating with her. The stress affected her health , and she began experiencing confusional migraines that caused blackouts while playing badminton. Her parents focused on helping her become independent and confident while learning to manage Type 1 diabetes. After medical tests and repeated episodes on the court, her family had to confront a difficult decision: continuing the sport was no longer a risk they could ignore. Giving up badminton was painful, especially after the sacrifices she had made to pursue it. Yet her parents encouraged her to keep moving forward, even when others doubted what she could achieve. Making room for independence Kiran and Shweta also made practical adjustments to help Kiara balance her studies and sporting ambitions. When the demands of school and intensive training became difficult to manage together, they decided to homeschool her in Grade 6. Her days included badminton practice, strength training and lessons with tutors, allowing her to continue her education without abandoning the sport she loved. Throughout these years, her doctor, Dr Atish Laddhad, remained an important source of guidance, helping the family navigate frightening episodes of low blood sugar. Her coaches and trainers also helped them understand when to push forward and when to step back. As Kiara grew older, she gradually took responsibility for managing her condition. Today, even when travelling alone, she makes sure she carries extra medical supplies, needles and syringes. With her parents' unwavering support, Kiara has built a career in sports, proving that a health condition need not define a child's dreams or future. For Shweta, that independence is part of what parenting has always meant: being present without making a child feel incapable. "I feel you should treat the child as a normal child and allow them to do normal activities, especially what they want to do," she says. Today, as a sports presenter, Kiara remains connected to the world she has loved since childhood. Her path may have changed from competing on the badminton court to talking about sport on screen, but her parents' belief in her has remained constant. Kiara's journey has not been without difficult choices or setbacks. But her parents have tried to ensure that diabetes remains something she manages, rather than something that decides her future. Today, Kiara is a sports presenter, hosting digital shows such as Bat, Ball Aur Baatein and Sports & The City. Their approach has been simple: understand the challenges, build a dependable support system, and give a child the confidence to discover what she can do. All images courtesy of Kiara Powar

items.titleOriginal: Generous Paternal Leave Policies Improve Maternal and Newborn Health, Family Finances, and Workplace Equality
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τη Megan Kuykendoll, καθηγήτρια οικογενειακής επιστήμης και κοινωνικής εργασίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Μαϊάμι, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Όταν γεννήθηκε το δεύτερο παιδί μας, ο σύζυγός μου είχε s…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Megan Kuykendoll , an instructor of family science and social work at Miami University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work. I’m a certified family life educator , and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work. So I was aware of the benefits his leave could have for our family — in theory. Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community. During his leave time, my spouse took our oldest child to playdates and birthday parties. He quickly became connected with our small-town network of families with kids close in age. I witnessed my spouse becoming more comfortable being the “main” parent in public, going to kid-centered community events, and connecting with other parents. Our family is still seeing the benefits of those few weeks 10 years later. Leave for supporting parents after the birth of a child isn’t standardized or required by law in most places in the U.S. Even countries with generous paid time off for the birthing parent don’t always offer similarly generous time for the non-birthing parent. This diversity in leave policies can make it hard to assess the impact of leave for the non-birthing parent. But existing research suggests that extended leave for birthing parents and moderate leave for non-birthing partners positively impact infant well-being and reduce postpartum mental health challenges. Maternal and Newborn Health Leave for both parents with the birth of a child can significantly benefit parental mental health overall and maternal mental health specifically . Paternity leave assists in the mother’s recovery and contributes to less of an increase in stress and depression than for mothers whose partners didn’t take leave. One Swedish study showed that flexibility within paternal leave policies, such as allowing new dads to take intermittent time off after the birth of a child, helped reduce the incidence of maternal postpartum health complications . Children also benefit from paternity leave. When a father takes significant leave — meaning at least two weeks — children report experiencing more father-child closeness and better communication in the relationship up to nine years later. And overall child health tends to improve when fathers take paternity leave. When paid leave policies are available for both mothers and fathers , breastfeeding is more likely to last longer. Longer breastfeeding is strongly linked to overall infant health and decreased infant mortality . SolStock—E+/Getty Images Paternity leave is an opportunity for fathers to become comfortable in their parenting role and connect with other parents. Family Balance Allowing both parents to have sufficient time off to bond and adjust to their new roles can also have longer-term benefits within the family unit and contribute toward more equity in child rearing. Even in 2026, mothers are often considered the “default” parent, with fathers taking a more secondary role . While fathers are more involved now than in previous generations, mothers are still more likely to be the first call from school. And even with an involved father, mothers continue to carry the invisible mental load of the family , an unseen burden of data, obligations, and preemptive planning tasks. This overreliance on mothers comes with a price: Mothers report being more stressed and tired than fathers do. As I experienced in my own family, when fathers have ample time off, it sets up the dynamic to be more balanced between parents. This helps reduce the strain on recovering mothers and redistributes some of the care work that goes into raising children. Home Economics What’s more, paid leave policies have been shown to help families’ financial health . Pay rates during leave can vary widely depending on your company, organization, or country. Without full or close to full pay, many families cannot afford to take leave. In the U.S., for example, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows time off, but not in all circumstances , nor is that time required to be paid. Many families cannot afford to take the full allowable time off, using up sick or vacation time if available. Many parents in the U.S. end up going back to work sooner than seems healthy . New parents in the U.S. often find themselves in an economic bind — they can’t afford to take leave, nor can they afford to rely on a single income to have a parent stay home. But many also can’t afford the childcare rates for newborns, which tend to be particularly high. National averages for infant care at childcare centers are nearly $200 more per month than toddler care. While rates vary significantly depending on where you live and what type of care you choose, infant care remains the most expensive . Despite the lack of a paid U.S. federal leave policy for parents, both domestic and multinational companies have noticed that their workers care about parental leave policies. Some have begun to offer leave for supporting parents in order to recruit and retain workers . Outside the US U.S. leave policies consistently rank at or near the bottom when compared with other similarly developed countries, like the 38 members of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, or OECD. Some countries follow a “use-it-or-lose-it” model of parental leave, where fathers in particular are encouraged to take a more substantial role in childcare. Sweden and Norway, for example, earmark 90 days of leave for each parent, and it cannot be transferred to or split with the other parent. This encourages both parents to take time off. There are many options across countries with parental leave policies. Flexibility and defined expectations seem to be key contributors to getting the most out of the parental leave that is offered. Cultural Adoption When non-birthing parents are men, another barrier to taking leave is the perceived social acceptability within their communities. Even when paid paternity leave is available, many men struggle to take it because of how traditional gender roles and expectations of masculinity frame childcare as women’s work . To offset these kinds of social pressures, countries like Japan and Austria offer incentives such as bonus leave time for families when fathers actually take their available leave. Germany offers a similar bonus, and it has found improved couple relationship satisfaction when fathers take more of their leave time. Beyond improvements in maternal and infant health, both parents taking leave can create a more equitable workplace environment . Disparities and discrimination that come when only women take leave after birth can lessen when fathers and other supporting parents also take leave. Childbearing women are then less likely to be penalized, formally or informally, for taking parental leave. Paid parental leave policies that provide leave for all parents, regardless of gender, also can help reduce structural inequality in the workplace across race and class. In the U.S., Hispanic and Black workers often have less access to paid leave policies and may experience increased pressure to return to work earlier than their white counterparts. As more states, countries, and corporations adopt more flexible and inclusive leave policies, researchers will continue to learn how parental leave benefits both parents and children. What they’ve found so far leads me to believe that, just like we’ve seen with prenatal care and early education programs , parental leave will prove to be an early investment in healthy children and families that pays dividends in the long term. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s something about crisp fall air that makes you want to get outside, and if you have a dog, you’ve probably noticed they feel it too: the extra pull on the leash when the leaves start to turn, the way they pause longer than usual to investigate every scent the new season brings. Dog trainer Sassafras Patterdale says fall is one of the best times of year to take your dog somewhere new, partly because the cooler temperatures make longer outings more comfortable, and partly because places like farmers’ markets, pumpkin patches , and hiking trails offer something a backyard walk can’t: a real chance for your dog to build confidence around new people, places, and experiences, while you practice skills like loose-leash walking around genuine distractions. A little planning goes a long way Before heading out anywhere new, Patterdale recommends thinking through your dog’s comfort level with crowds. Younger puppies and newly adopted dogs who are still building confidence tend to do better at quieter times, like weekday visits or early weekend mornings, while dogs who are comfortable around people and other animals may be ready for busier gatherings. Neither is wrong; it just depends on where your dog is right now. Pack a few essentials: water and a portable bowl, treats for rewarding good behavior, and poop bags. A properly fitted harness or collar and a standard six-foot leash are good to have in any busy area, and depending on the weather and your dog’s coat, a sweater or jacket may be a smart call for smaller or short-haired dogs. Farmers market A farmers market is one of the more dog-friendly fall outings. The mix of people, other animals, food smells, and steady foot traffic gives your dog plenty of opportunities to practice calm, attentive behavior on leash, and plenty of reasons to earn a treat. Patterdale recommends offering praise and treats whenever your dog walks calmly at your side or glances back to check in with you. Those little check-ins are what you want to encourage. Keep your dog close and prevent them from sniffing or pawing at food displays, and be mindful of shoppers who may not be comfortable around dogs. Most farmers markets welcome well-behaved, leashed dogs, but policies vary by location, so confirm before you go. Pumpkin patch A pumpkin patch visit makes for good seasonal photos, and dogs tend to enjoy the outing for their own reasons entirely. The open space, interesting smells, and steady stream of new things to look at give them a lot to engage with, and it’s a naturally good setting to practice cues like “stay” somewhere unfamiliar and exciting. Patterdale recommends checking the farm’s pet policy before arriving, since some farms restrict dogs in certain areas, particularly active harvest fields, for food safety reasons. Farms that host seasonal activities often welcome leashed dogs in the public areas, so a quick call or website check usually settles it. Corn maze If the farm also runs a corn maze, it can be a fun extension of the visit. The winding paths give dogs a chance to sniff and explore at their own pace, which Patterdale says is some of the best mental stimulation you can offer on a walk. One thing to watch for: avoid letting your dog round corners ahead of you, since that can startle other visitors, particularly children, or lead to an unexpected run-in with another dog. Haunted corn mazes are generally better skipped, since the loud noises and sudden surprises tend to be overwhelming for most dogs, even confident ones. As always, confirm the pet policy before you go. Hiking trail For a quieter option that lets you and your dog set your own pace, a fall hike is hard to beat. Many state and local parks welcome leashed dogs, and autumn trails give dogs a lot to work with: the crunch of leaves underfoot, the smell of damp earth, the cool air that seems to make dogs want to cover more ground than usual. Patterdale recommends allowing extra time so your dog can stop to sniff and investigate along the way. Dogs experience a huge portion of the world through their noses, and giving them space to follow a scent or linger over a fallen log makes the whole outing more satisfying for both of you. Check park regulations before heading out, since rules about dogs on trails vary by location and trail type. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Water has always been part of how many American cities move people, but for most of the country’s history it has been an afterthought compared to roads and rails. A new generation of electric ferries is beginning to change that, and some of them work in a way that is surprising: they handle the problem of water by getting out of it. The physics problem that held electric boats back Electrifying boats has always been harder than electrifying cars, and the reason comes down to drag. Water resists a moving vessel far more than air resists a moving vehicle, which means boats require substantially more energy per mile. That high energy demand, combined with the weight of batteries, has made it difficult to design an electric vessel that can carry enough passengers far enough to be useful as everyday transit. Hydrofoils get around this in a way that seems almost too obvious once you hear it. These vessels use underwater wings to lift the hull clear of the water as they accelerate, and once the hull is airborne, drag drops sharply. Vessev , a company that builds fully electric hydrofoil boats, says its design cuts drag by about 66 percent, which lets the boats carry smaller, lighter battery packs without sacrificing range. “We substantially reduce the drag that you feel, and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” said Eric Laakmann , Vessev’s chief executive and co-founder. What the ride is like The transition happens fast. As a Vessev boat accelerates through New York Harbor, the hydrofoils push the hull about a foot and a half above the surface, and the sensation of a boat working against waves gives way almost immediately to something smoother and quieter, closer to gliding than crossing water. “We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said during a recent demonstration, drawing curious looks from passengers on a nearby sightseeing ferry. His company is still a novelty to most people on the water, and he knows it. From demonstration to daily commute Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand, with Australia next and its first US route planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann’s ambition runs past tourism: he wants electric vessels to be as unremarkable as buses, something commuters use because it’s there. “More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said. That idea has already taken root in parts of Europe. Stockholm commuters are riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela, which says its design uses as much as 80 percent less energy than conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of the same boats for coastal service. The US is later to this shift, but several cities are starting to move. San Francisco prepares for a half-billion-dollar overhaul San Francisco carries about 3.5 million ferry passengers a year across a region shaped by its bay, and every one of the 18 vessels in the current fleet runs on diesel. Four battery-powered ferries are set to join the fleet over the next two years as part of an electric overhaul worth roughly half a billion dollars, including new charging infrastructure at its docks. Converting a ferry network is more complicated than swapping out a car fleet. Ferries run on fixed schedules and cannot stop mid-route to recharge, so operators have to design the entire system around the relationship between battery range, trip time, and how much power the shoreside chargers can deliver in the minutes a vessel sits at the terminal. Seamus Murphy, who runs the agency, put it plainly: “We have a lot of waterfront.” San Francisco’s new vessels won’t use hydrofoil technology , but the agency says they’ll make it the first ferry operator in the country to run high-speed, all-electric service. The economics of a fleet switch For a long time, the financial math and the environmental math didn’t add up at the same time. Battery-powered ferries cost more upfront, but electric motors tend to be more efficient than diesel engines, and the savings on fuel and maintenance accumulate. Rising diesel costs have shifted the balance, as has continued progress in battery technology. “You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time, and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” Murphy said. How well that holds up depends on the route: long distances, tight turnaround windows, and limited charging opportunities can all make the switch impractical. Not every waterway is suited to a fully electric vessel. For shorter commuter routes in cities with the right geography, though, the numbers are starting to work. For San Francisco’s expansion, both the boats and their batteries are being manufactured in the US. Murphy sees this as a window that won’t stay open indefinitely. “These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” he said. “We don’t want to be left behind.” Water as working transit Transportation is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the US, and watercraft burning diesel contribute their share, particularly around busy ports and waterfront neighborhoods. Electric ferries could cut both emissions and the localized air pollution that diesel docks generate, while also opening up routes that weren’t previously viable and connecting communities by water without the cost of new roads or rail. It won’t happen all at once. Some cities will move fast; others will take years to follow. But the direction looks clear. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said, standing on a boat that had just crossed a harbor without burning a drop of fuel. items.descriptionOriginal: Pretty much everyone would be overjoyed at the thought of being given some free money. But how much of that free money would you be willing to risk to double it ? It sounds like a question for the Las Vegas casinos. But they make their money with long odds, and games that seem winnable but usually aren’t. A classic riddle simplifies the equation and, in doing so, brings up a fascinating debate between human psychology and raw math. The two envelope problem explained Content creator Joey Rogoff recently shared something of a riddle on his Facebook page . “You’re given two envelopes. One contains exactly twice as much money as the other. You choose one and open it to find $100. You’re now offered the chance to switch envelopes. Would you switch?” It’s a variation on a classic prompt called the “two envelope problem.” In essence, the question says that you could walk away with $100, or you could choose the other envelope which has an equal shot at being either $50 or $200. What would you do? Joey Rogoff started quite a stir when he shared the two envelope problem. Joey Rogoff/ Facebook The mathematically correct answer is… The math behind the riddle is simple… at first. We assume the other envelope has equal odds of containing either $50 or $200. That puts the EV, Expected Value, of opening the other envelope at $125—it’s the average of the two possible outcomes. If you did the exercise a billion times, you’d come out ahead by switching. Simple. Where things start to get a little confounding is if you leave both envelopes closed. You select one, your chosen envelope, but don’t open it quite yet. If you are given the choice of switching in that split second before you find out what’s inside, the math says the same thing: The other envelope yields a 1.25 EV. So you switch, and choose the other one. But before you open that one, the math again suggests that you should switch back . See the problem? It creates an infinite loop. A paradox . Lucky for us, mathematicians have been hard at work on the two envelope problem for years. The problem with the logic above is that, in the real world, not all outcomes are equally likely. If the scenario were real, there would have to be a top limit, or a budget. There could be no infinity dollars inside one of the choices. So the bigger the number you’d find in your original envelope, the less likely you would be to want to switch; both because the odds that the other envelope contained double your already large amount get smaller, and because the potential loss would hurt far more. However, for Rogoff’s hypothetical version, where the first envelope contains $100, it feels like you should switch, even if the math behind it is a little murky. Psychology shows why the problem has people divided Even if you feel like switching is the right choice, your actions might get overridden by another feeling all together. A commenter on Rogoff’s post made a salient point when he wrote, “I fully understand the math logic in most of the other comments about switching, but I would stand pat. Whenever I have an either/or choice, I always make the wrong choice. Every time. I know no matter what I do will be wrong, so I would rather be wrong with $100 than with $50.” And this commenter wasn’t the only one. For every person who understood that the probability of walking away with more money was better with a switch, there was another person too afraid of losing the $50 to pull the trigger. “I’m taking the $100 and walking away. Most of y’all need to stay away from casinos.” “You can’t lose money you don’t win. Only on money you possess. That means keeping the $100 isn’t you losing $100 if you didn’t get the $200 by switching. You DO lose money if you switch and the other envelope only has $50” There’s clearly something larger at play in this problem than just mathematics. What the pure numbers don’t account for is something psychologists call loss aversion . It’s a cognitive bias that says the pain of losing something is worse than the joy of an equivalent gain. In this context, many people feel that losing out on $50 would not be worth the potential thrill of winning an extra $100. It’s a fascinating concept. Many experts argue that loss aversion holds us back and impairs our ability to make the best decisions in many areas of life: career, money, dating, friendships. But sometimes that deep fear of losing out protects us. For example, what if the two envelope problem wasn’t a hypothetical game, but a real scenario, and you needed the money to pay rent? Risking the switch would be difficult for most people in that scenario, even though the math would stay the same. The two envelope problem is such a classic because you can argue about it forever and never be wrong. It’s a fantastic litmus test for our risk tolerance, and even if the math gets a little shaky in hypothetical-land, your response to the riddle can tell you a lot about how you make decisions. The post The classic ‘two envelope problem’ riddle pits math against psychology appeared first on Upworthy .

Ένα ζευγάρι στο Λος Άντζελες δεν ταίριαζε. «Η μητέρα μου που γεννήθηκα ήθελε πραγματικά κάποιον ντόπιο, κάποιον στο Τέξας, κάποιον με τον οποίο θα μπορούσε ίσως να έχει σχέση», Thiele, η « Ενήλικες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Owen Thiele’s birth mother had already made her decision . She was in Texas, and she wanted her son placed with a family nearby, people she might be able to stay in touch with . A couple in Los Angeles didn’t fit. “My birth mom really wanted someone local, someone in Texas, someone who she could maybe have a relationship with,” Thiele, the “ Adults ” actor, said in September on Tish Cyrus’s podcast, “ Sorry We’re Cyrus .” Rather than leave it to the agency, she called the couple herself. “Eventually my birth mom called my mom, I think, as a courtesy to be like, ‘I’m kind of going in a different direction here,’” Thiele said. Nobody picked up so it went to the answering machine. The greeting was Thiele’s dad tickling his mom while she tried, and failed, to get through it without laughing. That’s all it took change everything. “My birth mom was like, ‘I need my son to be filled with laughter and joy, and I want him to be around… support and love,’” Thiele said. Her message to the couple was simple: “Come pick up your kid.” View this post on Instagram Thiele, now 30, also stars in Prime Video’s “ Overcompensating .” He and Cyrus had met at Raven-Symoné’s birthday party, where they figured out within minutes that they’d both been adopted at birth. He was born in Houston in 1996 and raised in Beverly Hills by music producer Bob Thiele Jr. and Amy Kanter. Growing up as a Black kid in a white Jewish family is now the basis of his upcoming comedy series, “ Off Color ,” which he’ll star in, write and co-executive produce. The post A birth mother called to reject an adoption. Their answering machine greeting changed her mind. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: A 1991 Wisconsin news report didn’t have high hopes for Gen X youth. We proved them wrong.

Έτσι, όταν το WMTV Channel 15, ένας ειδησεογραφικός σταθμός στο Ουισκόνσιν, δημοσίευσε μια ειδική αναφορά για το πώς ο Gen…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sometimes, it takes hindsight to figure out the essence of a generation. For example, the Boomers didn’t know while they were coming of age that their gen would lead to an explosive growth of the population. It often takes years to see and analyze the trends. So when WMTV Channel 15, a news station in Wisconsin, put out a special report of how Gen X was shaping up, it would be impossible to know if their predictions were correct. The year was 1991, when Gen X was entering college and early adulthood. (A few of the younger X-ers were just finishing up high school.) The exposé was focused on how, for the first time in American history, many of this 80s/90s generation were facing more hardship than their parents. View this post on Instagram ‘What TV news thought of Gen X’ A chyron reading, “What TV News thought of Gen X back in 1991” floats at the top of the clip , posted by 90s Rock Vault . Two news reporters sit behind a desk, the woman wearing an 80s-styled white blazer, complete with linebacker-sized shoulder pads. She shares, “This is the first generation facing adulthood believing that life for them may not be as good as it was for their parents. It’s creating a generation whose only reality is simply a future in doubt.” The clip cuts to a person wearing headphones as they lie on a backpack. Nirvana’s “Smells Like Teen Spirit” screams in the background, as the camera cuts to young people strewn across college campuses. “There is a sense of insecurity, which is probably realistic.” Another voice is heard saying, “And you worry about, you know, just getting a job.” The 13th Gen We hear the reporter add, “It adds up to a lot of anxiety that shows up in their music, their clothes and their attitude. Often misinterpreted and misunderstood, about the only thing they are certain of is that they are uncertain. They are Generation X, the 13th Gen.” They cut to an interview with Victor Ferrall, the then President of Beloit College. He explains, “If you start from Ben Franklin and count forward in American history, this is the 13th generation of Americans.” The reporter continues, “Growing up in the economic upheaval of the 70s and 80s, weaned on Sesame Street and MTV, most 20-somethings accept their unique situation. Their life will not be like their parents’.” We flash back to Ferrall, who further shares, “There’s a huge change in America. Just for the entire history of our country, people have always believed that life would be better for their children than it was for them.” Over photos of people walking down a busy street in the ’90s, the reporter adds, “…until Generation X. They watched inflation balloon their parents’ paychecks. And now they search for the real value in everything they do.” ‘Without all the hype’ She holds a microphone up to a young woman. “Realistic. ‘Real’ is the main thing that we’re looking at. Something that’s real with, yeah, without all the hype and the gimmicks and things like that. It’s our whole mentality.” Roseanne Cheeseman, of Directions Magazine, jokes, “That whole thing about waiting till you can get your big break into the burger industry. You know what I mean? And a lot of that is tongue in cheek. I think that a lot of the cynicism on the part of Generation X is not so much being 100 percent disillusioned with their chances in the world, but a lot of it is just making fun of the situation.” “Generation X,” the news reporter shares, “ponders whether the future holds happiness.” For that thought, they throw it over to Gerald Marwell, a Sociology Professor at University of Washington. “People in the ’60s,” he says, “had a pretty good idea…they thought that they were going to be like, in a sense, their parents. They were going to get married. They were going to have kids.” The divorce revolution When it came to Gen X, the concept of commitment was reimagined. Young adults dressed in red and black flannel shirts are shown as the reporter continues. “And while the flower children were protesting and fighting for social change, they started a revolution.” (“The divorce revolution,” Marwell states.) She relays, “Generation X grew up smack dab in the middle of it.” The report then interviews a young woman, wearing all black, her ear riddled with earrings. “A lot of people, I don’t think, expect to be happy in relationships. Cuz that’s what they saw.” Another woman adds, “I think a lot of people are leery of that and would like to have a longer relationship before they get into the commitment of marriage.” Marwell explains, “The kids today aren’t really sure what their lives are going to be like. They aren’t sure how many kids they’re gonna have. They’re not sure they’re gonna have any kids. They’re not sure of what’s going to happen to them.” Finally, Ferrall shares, “Parents had uncertain values to pass on to their kids. And economic uncertainty to pass on to them. And it left young people kind of rootless. Kind of unsure of themselves.” Gen X now Now, 35 years later, we have a true sense of how Gen X fits into the world. Despite the uncertainty, many are often quite successful. Kieran Smith writes, “After college, Gen X continued to succeed in the workplace, resulting in a generation financially outcompeting those around them. According to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median income of American workers reaches its peak between the ages of 45 and 54, roughly the age of most Gen Xers.” Generation X, despite the cynical jokes and often dark music, are also deemed by some to be the happiest generation. In a recent piece I wrote for Upworthy, I quoted Alene Dawson’s 2011 article “Study Says Generation X is balanced and happy,” for CNN. She cites University of Michigan’s The Generation X Report , which claims Gen Xers (who at the time were between 30–45) are ‘active, balanced and happy.’” Don’t let the grunge rock fool you. While some of us might have been handed a plate of lemons, we squeezed as much out as possible to make lemonade. The post A 1991 Wisconsin news report didn’t have high hopes for Gen X youth. We proved them wrong. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Generation X is known for being independent , self-reliant, and generally tough as nails. Many Gen Xers had to learn to fend for themselves from an early age, and as a whole, they developed a rather distant relationship with authority. While not everyone fits the stereotypes, it’s helpful for others to understand the norms and tendencies of different generations. The good news is that Gen Xers are pretty awesome if you’re on their good side. The better news is that getting on the good side of Gen X is really not that hard. 1: Motivate Gen X with two phrases, “Do it your way” and “Don’t sweat the rules” Many Gen X grew up in divorced single-parent homes. So were forced to be self-reliant and unsupervised early on. They want independence to get it done their way. — Michael Girdley (@girdley) April 5, 2022 ‘Mind hacks’ to use with Gen X Business creator Michael Girdley shared 10 tricks, or “mind hacks” on X to use with Gen Xers. Many of them apply to the workplace, but most can also carry over into other areas of life. Here are Girdley’s tips in a nutshell: Don’t make them follow rules Girdley says you can motivate Gen X with two phrases: “Do it your way” and “Don’t sweat the rules.” Gen X has always valued its independence. Now that they’re aging toward retirement, that’s only gotten more ingrained. 2. Send well-written emails Gen X grew up learning to write business letters with teachers who were sticklers for proper grammar. Xers may not like rules, but they appreciate good writing. 3. Acknowledge their emails quickly Gen X feels secure knowing what’s what and who’s responsible for things. Don’t leave them hanging. 4: Focus with Gen X on mission and results. Not seniority, effort, or hours worked. You’ll often hear Gen X say, “If someone gets the job done in half the time, that’s fine.” — Michael Girdley (@girdley) April 5, 2022 Gen X doesn’t care about arbitrary rules 4. Focus on mission and results Gen X cares about getting stuff done and doing it well. They don’t care about how long it takes or arbitrary rules and expectations for work times or hours. 5. Allow them to have a balanced life Work-life balance was pretty much invented by Gen X. They don’t want the workaholic life of their Boomer parents. 6. Bond with Gen X as individuals Independence also comes with individualism for Gen X. Don’t treat them like a monolith. (Yes, I see the irony in this list. Point still stands.) Millennials might see themselves as a tribe, and Boomers as an institution. Gen X are individuals, full stop. 7. Be direct Gen X likes data and facts. Cut the fluff and tell it like it is. 8: Just acknowledge Gen X exists. Gen X feels forgotten. Only 20% of the population. They’re also the people in your org with their heads down, getting stuff done. But, take them for granted and they can bolt. pic.twitter.com/jG91iK3b9r — Michael Girdley (@girdley) April 5, 2022 Gen X often gets forgotten 8. Acknowledge they exist Gen X is often called the “forgotten generation” for a reason. But as Girdley says, they are “the people in your org with their heads down, getting stuff done…take them for granted and they can bolt.” 9. Expect some pessimism Gen X has earned its sardonic sense of humor and slight air of cynicism. “Gen X is the first generation to NOT do as well financially as their parents or kids did,” writes Girdley. 10. Expect work-life separation In addition to work-life balance, Gen Xers like to keep their personal life distanced from their work life. They’ll be friendly at work, but may be reticent to make real friendships with colleagues. tl;dr: Win by doing these things with Gen X: 1) Say "Do it your way" 2) Use well-written emails 3) Say "I got it!" 4) Focus on the mission w/ them 5) Allow life balance 6) Bond as people 7) Be direct 8) Acknowledge they exist 9) Expect pessimism 10) Expect work-life separation — Michael Girdley (@girdley) April 5, 2022 Gen Xers are a pretty cool bunch as long as you understand how they function. They want to be seen and acknowledged, but they largely want to be left to their own devices. Contradictory? Maybe. Utterly and expectedly on brand for the latch-key kid generation? Absolutely. items.descriptionOriginal: A big discrepancy exists between how know-it-alls see themselves and how others see them. The average know-it-all probably thinks people respect them more because they are always right. However, research shows the opposite: folks who can admit they’re wrong and say, “you are right,” are seen as more likable and competent than those who think they know everything. A 2022 study from the University of Houston found that after reviewing a fight online, participants rated those who could admit they were wrong as more likable and competent than those who did not. A woman who made a mistake. Credit: Canva People like those who can admit they are wrong “Oftentimes, we’re trying to save face, especially on social media networks, where a lot of people can see our interactions; so, we might refuse to admit we’re wrong, because we’re afraid people are going to look down at us,” lead researcher Adam Fetterman, director of the Personality, Emotion, and Social Cognition Lab at the University of Houston, told Greater Good . “But, instead, what people like is intellectual humility—that someone is willing to change their opinion when they’ve heard new information.” The funny thing is that the person who won’t admit they are wrong does so, at least partially, to appear strong and intelligent. They want to be seen as competent, smart, and as someone who makes good decisions. However, research shows that taking a stand when you’re wrong makes you look less competent because you have poor critical-thinking skills and, most likely, a huge ego. Good listeners are more likable People who show intellectual humility by admitting when they’re wrong and someone else is right are more likable because they show they are good listeners. Studies show that being a good listener is one of the most likable traits you can have. Intellectually humble people also show they are open to new ideas, instead of being close-minded. A study from Baylor University found that after just 30 minutes of interaction, people rate those high in intellectual humility as more likable than those low in it. “The ability to admit we’re wrong helps us to update our beliefs in a more fact-oriented manner,” Fetterman continues. “So, let’s say, if we find out we’re wrong about COVID-19 or vaccines and can admit we’re wrong, maybe we’re going to end up in a better place.” A woman apologizing. Credit: Canva But that doesn’t mean that we should intentionally go around telling others they are right; you have to be genuinely intellectually humble. “If someone admits they’re wrong very quickly, you might think, ‘Hey, wait a second. We haven’t really even talked about this; you’re not even thinking or really engaging in this conversation,’” Fetterman continues. “That’s probably not a good idea.” When you tell someone they are right, it goes a long way because it shows you are a good listener, intellectually curious, and open-minded. You also have no problem taking yourself down a peg and giving the other person the respect they are due. Ultimately, people are much more impressed by someone who can admit they are wrong than by someone who will go to great lengths to demand they’re correct. In the end, know-it-alls seem to know everything, but the fact that they aren’t very popular. items.titleOriginal: Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το Open Campus. Περνώντας από το συμβουλευτικό γραφείο του New River μια μέρα, η Stephanie Addikis παρατήρησε ότι τα βιβλία ζωγραφικής και τα Lego που είχε βοηθήσει να αποθηκεύσουν σε ένα κοντινό κουτί ήταν… «πολύ αγαπημένα». Αυτό ακριβώς ήλπιζε ότι θα συμβεί. Το «απασχολημένο κουτί» με παιχνίδια είναι μέρος μιας νέας προσπάθειας στο New River για προμήθεια…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Open Campus . W alking by New River’s advising office one day, Stephanie Addikis noticed that the coloring books and Legos that she had helped stock in a nearby box were … “well-loved.” This was just what she was hoping would happen. The “busy box” stuffed with toys is part of a new effort at New River to support parenting students. When students are filling out the FAFSA or visiting with their adviser, they can bring their children and know they will have toys nearby to entertain them. “I don’t think we realized how many kids were coming on campus until we put these out, and now they’re really being utilized,” said Addikis, who is the adult career coach and community outreach specialist at New River. New River Community College is working to integrate more support for parenting students throughout campus. Courtesy of New River Community College A report released a couple weeks ago from The Institute for College Access & Success, or TICAS, showed that about a quarter of students attending rural-serving institutions are parents. But those colleges are also less likely to have childcare on campus than their non-rural counterparts. A lack of data on the number of parenting students is one of the biggest challenges for colleges trying to support them, according to one of the authors of that report, Erika Roberson. There’s a reason that Addikis was so excited to see used toys on campus: She does not know exactly how many parent students go to New River. While at least five states have now required public colleges to ask students if they have children, and Virginia just passed similar legislation this spring , the lack of standardized data collection makes serving these students even more difficult. And supporting them matters because student parents are more likely to be students of color, low-income and the first in their families to go to college. Those challenges combined make them less likely to graduate than their non-parenting peers. But, like rural places do, these colleges are getting creative in expanding support even with limited data and funding. To collect more thorough data, Roane State Community College in eastern Tennessee is partnering with Achieving the Dream . Others are collaborating with local churches, women shelters, groups like United Way and other nonprofits to connect student parents with resources. Our reporter at partner newsroom The Fort Worth Report, Dang Le, recently reported on new childcare centers that opened at Tarrant County College with the support of the college, county and a childcare nonprofit. “Not all these schools are receiving robust grants to do this work,” Roberson said. “Maybe there are existing partnerships that schools have that they might be able to tap into to more explicitly support their student parents, or maybe there are ways in which they can modify syllabi to include family-friendly policies that don’t have dollar signs on it.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Rather than one new program, it’s a cultural shift that student parents are looking for, according to another recent report focused on six public rural-serving colleges and universities in California . In other words, student parents want to feel seen — by their counselors, advisers, professors and other staff members or peers. While parents make up a large portion of students at rural-serving schools, it’s common for these students to still feel isolated . That’s why several colleges featured in the TICAS report are starting peer parenting groups and hosting events. New River, for example, has a dedicated family study room with child-sized furniture in their library (which also serves as a public library) and consistently hosts events or dinners for students and faculty with children. New River provides care packages for new and expecting parents, including diapers, wipes, a Walmart gift card and t-shirts. Courtesy of New River Community College Addikis said she felt this cultural shift even more prominently at New River when funding to parent-support programs decreased. New River was one of the first five colleges to receive the College Attainment for Parent Students grants from the Virginia Foundation for Community College Education. In those first couple of years, the college created cohorts of 20 student parents, and each parent was eligible for $2,000 stipends per semester, including summer semesters. Now, the foundation associated with the community college system gives each of the 23 schools some funding, so the grant amounts have decreased. New River adjusted by starting an application process, and they granted 17 students $500 each this year. Addikis said more than half of the students who applied said they rely on friends and family for childcare, so this stipend will likely help reimburse things like gas or food. But with fewer financial resources, Addikis started to look at what she could do to grow relationships with these student parents and remind them that they are not on their own. For example, she has a work-study student who is also a parent this semester, and that student is planning to start a student parent club on campus. The challenge, she said, still remains in increasing awareness about the resources on campus. One thing that she said helped was creating a section of their first-year orientation course specifically for adult learners and highlighting resources available for parents. “I see it now as a warm hug, and a lot of love and support and just a building of awareness,” she said, talking about how the parent support has changed with less funding. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Still, researchers like those at TICAS still advocate for increased data and funding for student parent support, especially on rural campuses. Two federal grant programs in particular focus on this area: Childcare Access Means Parents in Schools and Basic Needs for Postsecondary Students. “I don’t want policymakers to forget rural parenting students,” Roberson said. “And if policymakers are really interested in strengthening rural economies, I think it’s important that they also invest in rural parenting students.” The post Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: They left Sydney, Australia, to raise their children in India. And their twins helped them embrace their new home. Olivia and Andre had always imagined moving to India. Olivia is a teacher, while Andre runs a small business. They planned their move in 2022, but life had a surprise in store: twins! Born extremely prematurely, the children needed extra care. The couple decided to delay their move until the twins completed their health checks at the age of two. Once they were ready, the family finally made the move to India. Their biggest surprise? The children adapted to the heat, language and everyday way of life faster than their parents. Instead of comparing everything with Australia, Olivia and Andre followed their twins’ lead and embraced the experience with an open mind. Today, the family is proud to call India home. What they value most is the beautiful sense of community and the chance to give their children a different way of growing up. Sometimes, a new country doesn't just change where you live. items.descriptionOriginal: Every October, something extraordinary happens in the Maldives. Millions of dragonflies begin appearing across the islands, even though there is hardly any freshwater for them to breed in. Where are they coming from? Scientists believe many of these tiny travellers arrive from India, crossing hundreds of kilometres of open sea. Some may even continue their journey towards Africa. And here's what makes this so fascinating. The globe skimmer dragonfly ( Pantala flavescens ), also called the wandering glider, measures barely five centimetres and weighs around 300 milligrams. That's less than a gram! Yet this tiny insect may undertake one of the most remarkable journeys in the animal world, travelling thousands of kilometres with help from something familiar to all of us in India: the monsoon. But how does an insect so small cross an ocean without stopping? And why would it attempt such a journey in the first place? Scientists have spent years trying to answer these questions. The mystery of millions of dragonflies arriving in the Maldives In 2009, researcher R Charles Anderson published a study about something that had puzzled observers in the Maldives for years. Every October, enormous numbers of dragonflies appeared on the islands. But the Maldives has very little surface freshwater, making it an unlikely place for dragonflies to complete their life cycle. By studying when the insects appeared in India and the Maldives, Anderson found evidence suggesting they were travelling from southern India, covering approximately 500 to 1,000 kilometres. His findings, published in the Journal of Tropical Ecology , raised an even bigger possibility. What if the Maldives was simply one stop on a much longer journey towards East Africa? The answer appeared to be connected to the changing monsoon. It all begins with something as simple as a rain-filled puddle To understand why these dragonflies travel, we first need to understand where they raise their young. Many dragonflies lay their eggs in ponds and lakes. The globe skimmer has an unusual advantage: it can breed in temporary pools formed by rainfall. Think of the shallow puddles that appear in fields, open grounds and low-lying areas during India's monsoon. For this dragonfly, these pools can become nurseries. The female lays her eggs in the water, where the young dragonflies develop before emerging as adults. But these pools do not last forever. Once the rains stop, they begin drying up. So, as rainfall shifts from one region to another, the dragonflies move towards places where fresh water becomes available. India's southwest monsoon, which generally lasts from June to September, creates ideal breeding opportunities. And when the rains begin moving southwards, the dragonflies appear to follow. Measuring around five centimetres and weighing less than a gram, it is among the world's most widely distributed dragonflies. Photograph: (Bangalore Mirror) How can something weighing less than a gram fly across an ocean? Here's where the story becomes even more remarkable. If a dragonfly tried to cross the Indian Ocean by constantly beating its wings, it would soon run out of energy. So how does it manage? It may be doing something similar to what birds do: using favourable winds to help carry it forward. Anderson's research suggested that the insects travel with winds associated with a shifting band of clouds and rainfall near the equator. Scientists call this the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ. Simply put, it is a region where winds meet, creating changing weather patterns. As this region moves southwards after India's monsoon, it can bring winds that favour the dragonflies' journey. Anderson suggested that they may fly more than 1,000 metres above the ground, where helpful winds could carry them towards the Maldives. But there was still one important question. Could their tiny bodies survive such a long flight? In 2021, an international team of researchers led by Johanna S U Hedlund studied how much energy these dragonflies would need to cross the ocean. Using computer models, they found that the insects could save enormous amounts of energy by gliding through the air and flapping their wings only when necessary. According to their calculations, a dragonfly using a combination of gliding and wing-flapping could potentially remain airborne for around 230 hours under favourable assumptions. By comparison, continuously flapping its wings would exhaust its estimated energy reserves in roughly four hours. The research showed why the right winds could make such an extraordinary crossing possible. However, these figures come from computer models. Scientists have yet to directly track individual globe skimmers throughout the proposed ocean journey. From India to Africa, but the same dragonfly doesn't make the whole trip The Maldives may be only one part of the story. In 2023, researchers from IIT Kharagpur, including Sanat Ranjan Kumar, Amit A Pawar, Arnab Roy and Sandeep Saha, examined how winds and rainfall could connect the dragonflies' movements across the Indian Ocean. Their research suggested a possible migration route: October to December: Dragonflies leave India and travel towards the Maldives as seasonal winds change. January to March: Favourable winds and rainfall may help them move towards the Seychelles and mainland Africa. May to July: Strong winds over the western Indian Ocean, known as the Somali Jet, may help later generations travel from Africa towards India. Some dragonflies may breed in temporary rainwater pools along the way, including on islands where suitable conditions exist. And here is an important detail. The dragonfly that leaves India is not necessarily the one that returns. The journey is believed to unfold across several generations. One generation travels, reproduces where conditions allow, and its offspring continue the movement. Researchers estimate that four to five generations may be involved over a year, with young dragonflies emerging approximately 45 to 60 days after breeding. The Wandering Glider (#Pantala flavescens), or Globe Skimmer, is a #dragonfly species known as the world's longest distance #insect traveller, aptly named based on its migrating behaviour. #AareyForest #aareycolony #Aarey #SGNP #Odonata #saveaareyforest #Biodiversity #Mumbai https://t.co/Txu3Z7PdU0 — Rajesh Sanap (@RajeshVS87) August 24, 2022 A remarkable journey that still holds mysteries Scientists have pieced together this possible migration by studying dragonfly sightings, rainfall, wind patterns and the energy needed for flight. While the arrival of globe skimmers in the Maldives is well documented, much of the proposed journey between India and Africa remains a scientific hypothesis supported by modelling and observations. There is still plenty to discover about the exact routes they take, where they breed and how they choose the winds that carry them. But the research already gives us a fascinating way to look at something as familiar as the monsoon. The same seasonal rains that fill our ponds, fields and lakes may also help make an extraordinary journey possible for an insect small enough to rest on our fingertip. And the next time you spot a dragonfly after the rains, consider this: a creature that looks so delicate may be capable of travelling farther than we could ever imagine. Sources: 'High-flying dragons: how the globe skimmer migrates across the Indian Ocean' : By Neha Jain, Published on 10 November 2021 'Do dragonflies migrate across the western Indian Ocean?' : By R. Charles Anderson, Published on 10 July 2009 'Transoceanic migration network of dragonfly Pantala flavescens: origin, dispersal and timing' : By Kumar Sanat Ranjan, Amit A. Pawar, Arnab Roy, Sandeep Saha, Published on 21 June 2023

The supplement prevented psoriasis in mice and showed promising results in a small human trial, revealing an unexpected connection between cholesterol and autoimmune inflammation.

items.descriptionOriginal: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.

items.descriptionOriginal: Step off a busy Bengaluru road and into a tree-filled park, and the difference can be immediate. The harsh sun gives way to shade, and the air feels cooler. For a city once celebrated as India's Garden City, these green spaces have become especially valuable as concrete buildings and asphalt roads spread. But what if a park could help cool the streets around it, too? A 2026 study suggests that Bengaluru's parks are doing exactly that. Researchers found that their cooling influence can extend hundreds of metres beyond their boundaries. They also identified a surprising number that could help cities plan better parks: 2.49 hectares, or roughly six acres. How far can a park's cooling reach? Researchers Arpit Verma and Sonam Agrawal wanted to understand how Bengaluru's green spaces help reduce heat in the surrounding neighbourhoods. Their study, published in Advances in Space Research , examined 15 urban green spaces using satellite images collected during summer and winter. The findings were encouraging. Most parks showed a cooling effect of over 1 C in their immediate surroundings, even where buildings and roads covered more than 70% of the surrounding area. On average, this cooling extended approximately 186 to 246 metres beyond park boundaries, with stronger effects during summer. Think about what that could mean for a neighbourhood. A park's trees and vegetation may help reduce surface temperatures along nearby roads and built-up areas, benefiting spaces beyond those used by its visitors. Why trees make such a difference There is a simple reason parks tend to be cooler. Trees block sunlight from directly heating the ground. Plants also release moisture into the air, helping cool their surroundings. Concrete and asphalt behave differently. They absorb and retain heat, contributing to higher temperatures across heavily built-up neighbourhoods. This is part of what researchers call the urban heat island effect , where cities become hotter than their less-developed surroundings. Parks alone cannot resolve urban heat. Their effectiveness depends on vegetation, surrounding construction and the availability of space for green cover. Photograph: (News 18 Kannada) The Bengaluru study found that a park's ability to counter this heating depended on its size, shape and surrounding development. And that led researchers to an important question: How big should a park be to offer effective cooling? Why 2.49 hectares could be a useful benchmark The researchers discovered that bigger parks generally cooled a wider area. However, increasing their size did not always bring equally large improvements in cooling. Their calculations identified 2.49 hectares, approximately 6.15 acres, as an efficient size for cooling intensity, or how much a park reduces surrounding surface temperatures. For cooling a larger surrounding area, the suggested size was 5.29 hectares, or about 13 acres. These figures offer useful guidance for planners deciding how to use limited urban land. Bengaluru already has expansive green spaces such as Cubbon Park and Lalbagh. But residents across the city also need accessible greenery closer to their homes. The study suggests that thoughtfully planned neighbourhood parks could help, especially in areas crowded with buildings. What this means for Bengaluru's future There is one important distinction. The researchers measured land surface temperatures using satellites, rather than the air temperatures people experience. So, while the findings show how green spaces reduce surface heating, they cannot guarantee that every nearby street will feel a certain number of degrees cooler. The 2.49-hectare figure is also a planning benchmark, rather than a fixed rule for every park. BBMP is keen to reclaim Bengaluru's Garden City tag. Currently, 1408 parks gardens are being maintained by the civic body. While 1135 of them have been fully developed, work is on to beautify 273 #parks. #BBMP #Bengaluru https://t.co/LZuwUOEnXh — Maheshwar Rao.M, IAS (@GBAChiefComm) December 19, 2019 Still, the message for Bengaluru is valuable: protecting existing parks, planting trees and planning green spaces carefully can help tackle urban heat. For residents, a neighbourhood park is where children play, friends meet and people take their evening walks. The research shows that its benefits can travel beyond those familiar paths. And perhaps that is how Bengaluru can strengthen its Garden City identity: by ensuring that the greenery people enjoy inside a park can also help cool the neighbourhoods they call home. Sources: 'The interaction between urban heat island and urban parks: An in-situ measurement-based review' : By Semra Ogce, Huseyin Ogce, Siyu Yu, Robert D. Brown, Published on 31 May 2025 'Investigation of Urban Green Spaces as Potential Cooling Sources for Heat Mitigation in Bengaluru Metropolitan City, India' : By Arpit Verma and Sonam Agrawal, Published on 1 July 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe Reading Time: 3 minutes Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has helped saiga antelope rebound from about 20,000 to 4.6 million. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has produced one of the largest wildlife recoveries on record. Saiga antelope numbers have climbed from roughly 20,000 in the early 2000s to about 4.6 million in 2026. The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative has led this work since 2006. Altyn Dala means “golden steppe” in Kazakh. The initiative has helped protect 5 million hectares of grassland, an area larger than Denmark. It is also bringing back wild asses and wild horses that vanished from the region long ago. The saiga is a small antelope with a large, flexible nose that filters dust and warms cold air. Its herds migrate hundreds of miles across the steppe, a vast, dry grassland with few trees. By the early 2000s, those herds had nearly disappeared. After the Soviet Union collapsed, poaching surged across Central Asia. Hunters killed saigas for meat and for male horns, which sold for traditional medicine in Asia. Within about a decade, the population crashed by more than 95%. Five partners joined forces in 2006 to reverse that decline. Kazakhstan’s Committee for Forestry and Wildlife works with the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan. Fauna & Flora, the Frankfurt Zoological Society, and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds bring international support. Their first priority was stopping the killing. Ranger teams and aerial patrols now cover the saiga’s range. Sniffer dogs and customs training help catch horn smugglers at the border. Next, the partners needed to know where the herds went. Since 2009, researchers have fitted saigas with satellite tags to map their migrations. That data shows which areas need protection and when. New reserves followed the herds. The most recent, Bokey Orda-Ashiozek in western Kazakhstan, covers about 657,000 hectares. Wildlife corridors also link reserves through private land, under joint plans with landowners. The strategy faced its hardest test in 2015. During the spring calving season, more than 200,000 saigas died within weeks, over 60% of the global population. A 2018 study in Science Advances linked the deaths to a bacterium that turned deadly in hot, humid weather. Because poaching was under control, the surviving herds could rebuild. Aerial surveys each spring tracked the comeback. The 2024 count found about 2.8 million saigas, and the 2026 count reached roughly 4.6 million. That is about 230 times the low point. In December 2023, the IUCN Red List moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened. The Kazakh association’s director, Vera Voronova, called it one of the most successful land mammal recoveries ever recorded. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe means rebuilding the full community of grazing animals, not just one species. Kulan, a wild ass native to Central Asia, disappeared from the Torgai steppe more than 100 years ago. Scientists consider them a keystone species, since their grazing and movement help shape the grassland. Reintroductions began in 2017, and partners aim to establish about 100 kulan in the region. A recent group traveled 2,139 kilometers by road from Altyn-Emel National Park. After a year in an acclimatization pen, the animals went free in August 2025. Przewalski’s horses are following the same path. Considered the last truly wild horse species, they vanished from the wild by 1969 and survived only in zoos. In Kazakhstan, they had been gone for about 200 years. Przewalski’s horses returning to the wild are part of restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe after about 200 years. Photo by Wijs (Wise) on Pexels. The first seven horses arrived at the Altyn Dala reserve in 2024. More followed in 2025 from Prague Zoo and Hungary’s Hortobágy National Park. In May 2026, five of them left their pens and began roaming free. Officials plan to bring 40 to 45 horses by 2029, enough to sustain the herd. A stallion named Galvan wears a GPS collar so rangers can follow his movements. Local support makes these gains last. The initiative runs education programs in rural schools and has published children’s books about steppe wildlife in Kazakh. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe depends on the next generation valuing these animals. Recovery has also created new tensions. Farmers in several regions report that saigas damage crops and compete with livestock for pasture. Authorities are now studying how to manage herd sizes without undoing two decades of conservation. Roads, railways, and fences still break up migration routes. Wildfires and farm expansion put pressure on ground-nesting birds. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe will require balancing people and wildlife for years to come. Twenty years ago, the saiga seemed headed for extinction. Today, millions roam the plains, joined by wild asses and horses returning after a century or more. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe shows what patient, well-coordinated protection can achieve. The post Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.
