items.description: Μια τεράστια μελέτη σε περισσότερους από 120.000 ηλικιωμένους δείχνει ότι τα κοινά φάρμακα για την οστεοπόρωση μπορεί να μειώσουν τον κίνδυνο της νόσου του Αλτσχάιμερ και άλλων άνοιων έως και 24%. Τα εκπληκτικά ευρήματα αυξάνουν την πιθανότητα ότι φάρμακα που χρησιμοποιούνται ήδη για την ενίσχυση των οστών θα μπορούσαν επίσης να βοηθήσουν στην προστασία του γερασμένου εγκεφάλου.
items.descriptionOriginal: A massive study of more than 120,000 older adults suggests that common osteoporosis drugs may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias by up to 24%. The surprising findings raise the possibility that medications already used to strengthen bones could also help protect the aging brain.

items.descriptionOriginal: As winter approaches, the air across several Indian cities is likely to become harder to ignore. Smoggy mornings, hazy skies, and rising pollution levels often prompt families to rethink the air they breathe at home. Suddenly, an air purifier begins to look less like a luxury and more like a practical addition to the living room or bedroom. But walk into a store or browse online, and you will find air purifiers promising everything from cleaner air to near-total particle removal. One term appears repeatedly: HEPA. So, what does it actually mean? And how do you know whether the air purifier you are considering will do its job? Here are five things worth checking before you bring one home. 1. First, understand what HEPA means HEPA stands for High-Efficiency Particulate Air. In simple terms, it refers to a filter designed to trap tiny particles suspended in the air as it passes through the filter. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), a HEPA filter can theoretically remove at least 99.97% of airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns. To put that into perspective, a micron is one-millionth of a metre. These particles can include fine dust, pollen, mould spores and smoke particles. This makes HEPA filtration particularly useful when outdoor pollution finds its way indoors or when household dust and allergens become a concern . Choosing an air purifier with the right Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR) can make a difference to how effectively it cleans the air in a room. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) However, not every product that mentions HEPA necessarily meets the same standard. Terms such as "HEPA-type" and "HEPA-like" do not, by themselves, establish that a filter meets a recognised HEPA performance specification. What to check: Look for a clearly stated filter grade and supporting performance information, rather than relying on the word HEPA alone. 2. Choose a purifier that suits your room Imagine buying a powerful air purifier for your bedroom, only to find that it struggles to clean the air in your larger living room. The problem may not be the filter itself, but the amount of air the machine can process. This is where CADR, or Clean Air Delivery Rate, comes in. It tells you how much filtered air a purifier delivers over a given period. A higher CADR generally means the machine can clean the air faster , provided the room size and other conditions are comparable. A purifier with a highly efficient filter may still be less effective in a large room if its airflow is insufficient. What to check: Match the manufacturer's recommended room size and CADR to the space where you plan to use the purifier. A bedroom and an open-plan living area may need different capacities. 3. Remember that HEPA filters do not remove everything HEPA filters are designed to capture particles, not every type of air pollutant. They do not, on their own, remove most gases, volatile organic compounds (VOCs) or odours. For instance, cooking can release particles into the air, while certain paints, cleaning products and new furniture can release gaseous chemicals. An activated-carbon filter can help adsorb some gases and odours. This is why some air purifiers combine HEPA filtration with activated carbon to tackle different kinds of indoor pollutants. While HEPA filters capture airborne particles, activated-carbon filters help tackle certain gases, chemicals and household odours. Photograph: ( Livemint ) What to check: If odours or gaseous pollutants are a concern, look for a purifier with an activated-carbon stage in addition to its particle filter. Check the manufacturer's specifications for what it is designed to remove. 4. Check the cost and availability of replacement filters Buying the machine is only the first expense. Filters collect particles over time and eventually need maintenance or replacement to keep the purifier working effectively. Replacement intervals vary depending on the model, how often it runs and the pollution levels in your surroundings. A filter used through a heavily polluted winter may need attention sooner than one used in cleaner conditions. What to check: Before purchasing, find out the price of a compatible replacement filter, whether it is readily available and how often the manufacturer recomm ends replacing it. Also check which parts can be cleaned and which must be replaced. 5. Look beyond the filter when comparing models A good filter is important, but the machine around it matters, too. Noise levels can affect whether you are comfortable running it at night, while energy consumption can influence your electricity bill if you use it for several hours each day. It is also worth checking the manufacturer's safety information. Some air-cleaning technologies, particularly ozone-generating devices, can introduce pollutants rather than simply remove them. Understanding how different filters work can help families make informed choices about improving indoor air quality. Photograph: ( MarketWatch ) What to check: Compare noise levels , power consumption, warranty, service support and safety specifications. Choose a model you can comfortably run and maintain as recommended. Cleaner air starts with informed choices As pollution levels rise, wanting to make the air at home a little cleaner is understandable. For families, it could mean being more mindful of the air children play in, the bedrooms where everyone sleeps, and the spaces where they spend most of their day. An air purifier can be one part of that effort. Taking a little time to understand the filter, choose the right model and maintain it well can help you make a more informed choice for your home. After all, cleaner indoor air begins with knowing what you are bringing through the door. Sources: 'What Is a HEPA Filter — and Does Filter Grade Actually Matter?' by Karban, Published on 11 April 2026. 'What is a HEPA filter?' by EPA. 'The HEPA Air Purifier: What You Need to Know!' by IQ Air, Published on 30 March 2017.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News American Red Wolf Pups Fostered into the Wild in North Carolina Reading Time: 3 minutes American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild bring fresh genes to a critically endangered species. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild mark a first in Saint Louis Zoo history. Three critically endangered, zoo-born pups now live with a wild Red Wolf family in North Carolina. Fewer than 40 American Red Wolves remain in the wild. They live only in northeastern North Carolina. That group would not even fill a single school bus. The wolves are critically endangered, which means they face a very high risk of extinction. Hunters nearly wiped them out in the 1800s and 1900s. They once roamed the southeastern United States and are native nowhere else. In the 1960s, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) teamed up with North American zoos. Together, they started a breeding and reintroduction program for the species. The three pups were born at the zoo’s Sears Lehmann, Jr. Wildlife Reserve. Staff collected them on April 20, when they were seven days old. They underwent a health exam before the trip. Zoo staff traveled with the pups to the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge in northeast North Carolina. They cared for the pups hour by hour along the way. FWS biologists then placed them in a wild den, a shelter where a mother raises her young. Biologists watched the den to see whether the wild mother returned. She did, and she accepted the newcomers into her litter. Several months later, the pups began exploring outside the den, and trail cameras showed all three alive and thriving. This process is called fostering. A wild mother raises pups born elsewhere as part of her own litter. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild add new genes to a very small population. Genetic diversity helps a population stay healthy. It improves disease resistance and reduces the harm of inbreeding, which happens when close relatives breed. Timing is the biggest challenge. A foster must happen within the first 14 days of a pup’s life. That is when wolf mothers bond with their young and are most likely to accept new pups. Two groups share the work behind American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild. FWS monitors breeding among wild wolves. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) Program guides breeding among wolves in zoos. When a wild litter is born, SAFE looks for zoo-born pups within that narrow window. In 2026, the Saint Louis Zoo’s litter was the only one born in professional care. Partnerships between zoos and wildlife biologists make American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild possible and bring new genes to a very small population. Photo courtesy of Saint Louis Zoo . Professional care means wolves living in zoos and similar facilities. These American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild were the only eligible pups in North America. Regina Mossotti leads the SAFE American Red Wolf Program and serves as the zoo’s vice president of animal care. She says every pup counts when fewer than 40 wolves remain. She sees fostering as a key way to give these pups a chance to support the species’ future. Emily Weller coordinates the FWS Red Wolf Recovery Program. She says several recovery actions rely on close teamwork with SAFE. The American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show how zoo partnerships directly help wild wolves. The wild mother had a large litter. The zoo cross-fostered a few of her pups into its litter at the reserve. This swap helps ensure she can care well for each pup. The exchange also moves genes between wild wolves and zoo wolves. Experts call that a rare and valuable chance for species recovery. The reserve covers 355 acres, roughly 270 football fields, and is closed to visitors. Wolves there learn survival skills with minimal human contact, preparing them for a possible life in the wild. In 2021, the zoo announced plans to develop about 20 acres for wolf conservation. Today, the reserve holds seven habitats for breeding and conservation. The zoo will share photo and video updates on its social media pages and website. Federal biologists continue to support the wild population through the national red wolf recovery effort. Each of the American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild strengthens a population found in only one region. Other reintroduction projects show similar promise, such as efforts to return gray wolves in Colorado . Careful releases and strong partnerships can help wildlife recover. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show what shared effort can achieve. Zoo staff, federal biologists, and a wild mother each played a role. The post American Red Wolf Pups Fostered into the Wild in North Carolina appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When rising water threatened a Sarus Crane's nest in Madanpura village in eastern Uttar Pradesh, two men stepped in. Local volunteer Chedi Kewat alerted the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) and worked with field assistant Ravindra Kumar Tripathi to secure the nest using bamboo poles. Thirty-one days later, the eggs hatched. It was one small rescue, but it tells us something important about India's birds . Their survival can depend on the pond beside a village, the marsh near a farm or the muddy shoreline along a coast. And that is why a new national assessment of India's birds matters. On 19 October 2026, WTI announced that experts had begun assessing 1,211 bird species regularly found across India. More than 100 preliminary assessments had been opened for expert review. Among them, three wetland birds, the Sarus Crane, Marbled Duck and Grey Plover, offer a glimpse of what is at stake. Why a pond beside a farm could decide a crane's future The Sarus Crane, the world's tallest flying bird, often makes its home in flooded paddy fields, village ponds and shallow wetlands. During the monsoon, these places provide space to build nests and raise chicks. But when marshes are drained, pesticides threaten birds or power lines cross their habitat, their survival becomes harder. Wetlands must remain places where birds can feed, rest and breed. These same habitats can also help nearby communities by recharging groundwater and reducing the impact of floods. Photograph: (ICIMOD-India Water Portal) The Sarus Crane has been proposed as Vulnerable in India's new assessment, indicating a high risk of extinction in the wild nationally. Uttar Pradesh has an estimated 19,000-plus Sarus Cranes. Across 10 eastern districts, WTI works with farmers, local volunteers called Sarus Mitras and village committees to monitor nests and protect wetlands. These community efforts matter because many crane nesting sites lie beyond protected wildlife reserves. The duck with fewer places to spend winter Every winter, the Marbled Duck travels to India in search of shallow freshwater wetlands where aquatic plants provide food and shelter. It has been recorded in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab and other states. But its proposed national conservation status is Endangered. Marshes are being drained, water bodies are changing and suitable habitats are disappearing across parts of its range. Because these ducks move between wetlands depending on water conditions , experts also need better monitoring to understand how their populations are changing. A bird that crosses continents, but faces a worrying decline The Grey Plover makes an extraordinary journey every winter, travelling from its Arctic breeding grounds to India's coastline. Here, it searches for food in coastal mudflats, where the retreating tide exposes small creatures. The exercise is being jointly undertaken by the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), the IUCN SSC Centre for Species Survival India–Wildlife Trust of India (CSS India–WTI) and the State of India's Birds (SoIB) Photograph: (Chuck Homler, Focus On Wildlife) Its proposed national category is Least Concern. That sounds reassuring, but another assessment raises questions. The State of India's Birds 2025 update estimated a 78.99% decline in its long-term population trend in India. Globally, the species is classified as Vulnerable. This difference shows why experts must carefully examine population records and habitat changes before finalising a bird's conservation status. What protecting these birds really takes India's new assessment will examine where birds live, how many there are and whether their populations are changing. Birdwatchers' sightings and field research can help experts fill information gaps. But identifying a bird's risk is only one part of protecting it. Wetlands must remain places where birds can feed, rest and breed. These same habitats can also help nearby communities by recharging groundwater and reducing the impact of floods. For Arshad Hussain, who works with local communities through WTI's Sarus conservation project , some of the happiest moments come when a farmer calls to report a new nest or a hatched chick. In Madanpura, protecting one Sarus nest meant recognising the danger in time and acting together. Across India, that same care for everyday wetlands could give many more birds a better chance. Sources: 'India Launches Collaborative National Red List Assessment of 1,211 Bird Species' : By Wildlife Trust Of India, Published on 19 October 2026 'Transitioning Wintering Shorebirds to Agroecosystem: A Thorough Evaluation of Habitat Selection and Conservation Concern' : By Diversity-Biodiversity Conservation, Published on 29 December 2023 National Wetland Inventory and Assessment (NWIA) Atlas 'Mercury contamination: a hidden threat to long-distance migrant shorebirds in critical wintering sites on the west coast of India' : By K A Rubeena , K M Aarif, Published on 23 September 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: Turn on a tap to wash your hands. Notice how much water hits your palms, bounces off and disappears down the drain. Now imagine this happening hundreds of times a day across an office building, alongside hidden leaks and cooling systems that use millions of litres of water. How much of it is actually being used, and how much is simply going to waste? Chennai-based, IIT Madras-incubated startup EarthFokus is trying to answer that question. Founded in 2019 by Arun Subramanian and Rishi Vandan, the water-tech company helps commercial buildings monitor consumption, identify leaks, recover water lost through evaporation and reduce everyday usage. Its three solutions, WaterOS, EcoVapure and WaterFokus, tackle different parts of the problem. Together, the company says, they have helped over 130 commercial buildings save more than five billion litres of water. It began with a tap EarthFokus started with a small experiment. In 2019, Arun, an engineer, was approached by a neighbour who wanted to explore ways to reduce water consumption in their garden. Around the same time, Chennai was facing its Day Zero water crisis, when the city's reservoirs ran critically low. The crisis brought home the importance of conserving water, but Arun began by looking at something much more ordinary: a tap. A conventional tap can release around 10 to 12 litres of water per minute, says Rishi. Yet, while washing our hands, much of that water can bounce off our palms and flow away unused. The team developed a fixture that could bring the flow down to as little as 0.5 litres per minute. The idea was to use only as much water as the task required. The product attracted attention during the COVID-19 pandemic, when frequent handwashing became essential. EarthFokus also secured early orders from corporate clients, including Cognizant. What began as an experiment to reduce tap water flow grew into a water conservation startup incubated at IIT Madras. But the founders encountered an unexpected hurdle. Customers often viewed the fixture as just another plumbing accessory, rather than a solution that could reduce a building's water consumption. "We had to change that perspective," says Rishi. "I'm not a dealer or a trader who's pushing products to you. Rather, we're a solution provider who wants to enable reduction at your building." That realisation pushed EarthFokus beyond taps. Instead of simply selling water-saving products, the team began helping clients measure consumption and verify the savings their interventions delivered. Three ways buildings can stop wasting water As the startup worked with more buildings, it realised that inefficient taps were only one part of the problem. Hidden leaks, poor monitoring and water lost through cooling towers offered other opportunities for conservation. 1. WaterOS: Spotting leaks before they become bigger problems Think of WaterOS as a monitoring system for a building's water supply. The platform uses IoT-enabled flow meters and sensors installed at key points, including supply lines, floors, washrooms and cooling towers. These continuously collect data and send it to the cloud, giving facility managers a near-real-time picture of how water is being used. AI then helps identify unusual patterns. For instance, a restroom might typically see heavy water use during office hours and almost none overnight. If the system detects a steady flow at 2 am, it can flag the anomaly for investigation. The cause could be a running toilet or a leaking valve that might otherwise go unnoticed for weeks. Unlike a monthly water bill, which reveals consumption after the fact, this system helps teams identify potential problems sooner. WaterOS uses smart sensors and real-time monitoring to help commercial buildings detect leaks and track water consumption. The technical team explains that WaterOS learns normal consumption patterns based on factors such as time of day, occupancy and seasonal variation. It can then flag deviations for facility managers to investigate. This makes it easier to move from reacting to a problem after water has been wasted to identifying it earlier. 2. EcoVapure: Recovering water from cooling towers Some of the biggest water losses in commercial buildings happen where occupants rarely look. Cooling towers, used in offices, factories and data centres, remove heat by allowing water to evaporate. While this is an essential part of the cooling process, it also means water is continuously lost. Cooling towers also lose water when some is drained away (blowdown) or carried away as tiny droplets (drift), although evaporation is often the largest source. EarthFokus developed EcoVapure to recover some of that water. Its deployed technology, called Capture, is designed for cooling towers that produce a visible plume of water vapour. As the plume passes over a specially designed surface, droplets gather and grow until they fall back into the cooling system. The recovered water can also be collected separately for other uses. The company says the technology can recover roughly 30% of evaporation loss under relevant operating conditions, though the actual amount depends on the tower and its operating environment. EcoVapure captures water droplets from cooling tower plumes, helping buildings recover a portion of the water otherwise lost through evaporation. EarthFokus is also developing Convert, a second approach intended to recover water from cooling towers without visible plumes. For Rishi, the opportunity extends beyond individual buildings. Cooling towers are used across industries, including power generation and data centres, making water recovery a potential way to address losses in essential infrastructure. 3. WaterFokus: Saving water without changing habits WaterFokus focuses on reducing water use at the tap. Its fixtures and aerators control the flow of water while maintaining the feel of a strong stream. "Aerators do this by mixing air into the water as it exits the tap, while other low-flow fixtures use restrictors or specially designed nozzles," adds Siva T from the cooling towers tech team. The difference may be barely noticeable while washing your hands. But across hundreds or thousands of taps used repeatedly throughout the day, even small reductions can add up. The idea is to make conservation almost effortless : install the fixture, and less water is used without asking people to change their routines. WaterFokus aerators reduce water flow while maintaining a comfortable stream, helping save water without changing everyday habits. EarthFokus also manufactures its fixtures in metal, with durability in mind, rather than relying on plastic products that may need frequent replacement. Together, the three solutions address different aspects of water management: WaterOS helps buildings understand where water is going, EcoVapure recovers some of what is lost, and WaterFokus reduces consumption at the source. How tracking water helped a building spot wastage One of EarthFokus's clients is WeWork India, which previously relied on manual readings to track water consumption across its centres. The process was labour-intensive, and the data often arrived too late to help facility teams identify unusual patterns quickly. With IoT-based metering, WeWork now has a more continuous picture of its water use. "The biggest shift has been moving from estimated, manual figures to accurate, real-time data across every asset," says P. Seshashayan, Manager, Energy & Sustainability, WeWork India Management Ltd. According to the company, consumption fell from 45 litres per person per day to 29 litres. WeWork has set a target of reaching 20 litres per person per day by FY28. WeWork's team says real-time monitoring has also helped it identify unusual consumption patterns sooner and strengthen sustainability reporting. It is currently evaluating EarthFokus's aerators and considering water audits, but has not deployed EcoVapure. For Rishi, the impact becomes especially meaningful when he can put the numbers into perspective. EarthFokus combines smart monitoring, water recovery and low-flow fixtures to tackle water wastage across commercial buildings. "I've spent multiple interactions with clients visualising this five-billion-litre number," he says. He recalls thinking about how that volume could have helped cities facing water shortages, including Bengaluru during its recent water crisis. For him, the number represents both a milestone and an opportunity to do more. EarthFokus is exploring how cooling-tower recovery could add significantly to its savings as the technology scales. The company has also worked with IBM and Cognizant. Rishi recalls that introducing water-saving fixtures at Cognizant's Chennai operations helped cut daily water demand by nearly 80%, according to the company's account of the intervention. These experiences have reinforced an important lesson for the founders: measuring water use is only the beginning. The next step is to make changes, verify their impact and keep improving. How the startup plans to save even more water EarthFokus typically begins working with a building by assessing its water infrastructure and establishing a baseline for consumption. It then identifies potential reductions and introduces monitoring or other interventions, allowing facility teams to track progress. The approach also reflects a practical understanding of what encourages businesses to invest in conservation. Alongside environmental impact, solutions need to improve operational efficiency and deliver measurable results. From a single tap to more than 130 commercial buildings, EarthFokus's solutions have helped save over five billion litres of water. Looking ahead, EarthFokus wants to expand EcoVapure and develop a water-recovery technology that can be adopted in India and scaled internationally. For Rishi, however, the underlying problem remains simple. Whether it is a tap, a reverse-osmosis system or a cooling tower, we often use more water than we actually need. "The basic problem is that we end up using more than what we need because we take water for granted," he says. For him, conserving water begins with understanding where the water we already have is going and finding ways to prevent it from being wasted. All images courtesy of EarthFokus team

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Εάν η σελίδα σας For You ήταν γεμάτη από άτομα που ακυρώνουν ραντεβού για μπότοξ επειδή άρχισαν να τρώνε περισσότερο σολομό, έχετε βρει την τάση "eat your skincare". Η υπόθεση είναι ότι η σωστή διατροφή μπορεί να κάνει αυτό που υπόσχεται ένα ντουλάπι φαρμάκων γεμάτο ορούς. Είναι, ειλικρινά, ελκυστικό… αλλά είναι επίσης μόνο εν μέρει tr…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If your For You Page has been full of people canceling Botox appointments because they started eating more salmon, you’ve found the “eat your skincare” trend. The premise is that the right diet can do what a medicine cabinet full of serums promises. It is, honestly, an appealing one… but it’s also only partly true. The route food takes to your skin When you eat, nutrients get absorbed in the GI tract and travel through the bloodstream to wherever your body decides to send them. There’s no targeting involved, so your skin gets what’s available once everything else takes its share. Topical skincare works on a different logic entirely, putting concentrated ingredients directly on one spot without the detour. “Wrinkles and collagen loss are multifactorial,” says Dr. Kseniya Kobets , Director of Cosmetic Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. “No single food or supplement is going to make a huge difference if the rest of your diet is poor, you are unhealthy or dealing with inflammation, excessive sun exposure or you don’t have a good skincare regimen.” Food can correct deficiencies that slow things down. Vitamin C and amino acids matter for collagen formation; fatty acids support the skin barrier. But more doesn’t mean more. “I think of it as filling the tank,” Dr. Kobets says. “You need the nutrients and building blocks, but overfilling it doesn’t make the collagen-making machinery work faster.” Too much vitamin C, she notes, can cause GI problems and, in some people, raise the risk of kidney stones. Can food protect you from the sun? Some of the content goes further: eat your sunscreen . That sounds ridiculous, but there’s real science underneath it. “There is interesting evidence around oral photoprotection ,” Dr. Kobets says. “Certain carotenoids, polyphenols and Polypodium leucotomos extract have been studied for increasing the skin’s resistance to UV-induced damage.” That’s not a reason to put the SPF away, though. “I sometimes think of these as an extra layer of defense, but definitely not an oral sunscreen,” she says. “No amount of blueberries, green tea or antioxidant supplements is going to replace properly applied and reapplied sunscreen, protective clothing and smart sun behavior.” What to eat for skin health If you want your diet to pull some weight here, the list is manageable. Dr. Sapna Palep , a dermatologist at Journelle Skin, recommends eggs, avocado, flaxseeds, walnuts, salmon, and dark chocolate, which between them cover protein, healthy fats, omega-3 fatty acids , and antioxidants. “Nutrition can influence inflammation, oxidative stress, the microbiome and skin-barrier function,” says Dr. Kobets. “What is good for your overall metabolic health tends to be good for your skin as well.” That’s the version of this trend that holds up: eating well really does support your skin, and the foods involved are things most of us would benefit from eating more of anyway. What food can’t do is replace sunscreen or stand in for a routine that’s doing something. Think of it as filling a role, not playing every position. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM History was made in governors’ races across the country on November 3. In ten states, voters chose candidates who had never held that office before as a matter of historical record, not just political preference: a Black woman elected to the governorship for the first time anywhere in the United States, the first Native American woman to lead any state, the first Latina governor of Texas, the first elected Latino governor of California, the first Black governors of Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin, and the first women ever to win governor’s races in Tennessee, Minnesota, and Ohio. The wins came from both parties and from states that historically appeared to share very little common ground politically, which is part of what made the night so hard to categorize. Georgia elects the first Black woman governor in U.S. history The result that will end up in history books is from Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s race to become the first Black woman ever elected governor of any U.S. state. The country had never crossed this threshold before, not in 250 years of gubernatorial elections. Lance Bottoms is 56 and served as mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022 before moving to Washington as an adviser to former President Joe Biden. Her defeat of Republican health care executive Rick Jackson also makes her the first Democrat to win a Georgia governor’s race in more than two decades, in a state that has been in political motion since it flipped in the 2020 presidential race. New Mexico’s Deb Haaland becomes the first Native American woman governor New Mexico voters sent Deb Haaland to the governor’s office, making her the first Native American woman to hold that position in any state. Haaland, who is of Pueblo Indian descent, has been making this kind of history for most of her public career. She was among the first Native American women elected to Congress, and later became the first Native American cabinet secretary when President Biden appointed her as Interior secretary. Her defeat of Republican Gregg Hull is one more memorable and significant accomplishment. Latino firsts in California and Texas California and Texas, the two most populous states in the country, will each have a Latino governor for the first time. In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra , who served as state attorney general before becoming Biden’s Health and Human Services secretary, defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom. It was not a close race, but it crossed a threshold the state had never crossed despite having one of the largest Latino populations in the country. Texas is the bigger surprise. Democrat Gina Hinojosa , a state representative, defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, one of the country’s most prominent conservative governors and a close ally of President Trump. Hinojosa is now both the first Latina governor of Texas and the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. Texas has been changing as its Latino population grows, and Tuesday’s result suggested that shift is now showing up at the top of the ballot. Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin each elect their first Black governors Three more states elected their first Black governor on Tuesday, and these wins came from both sides of the aisle. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Trump, defeated Democrat David Jolly to succeed outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has served in Congress since 2021 and spent two terms in the state legislature before that; he campaigned on affordability and pledged to continue Florida’s conservative direction. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford , the state’s attorney general, defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo to become the first Black governor of any state west of the Mississippi River. Ford had already been Nevada’s first Black Senate majority leader and its first Black attorney general; he first won a state legislature seat in 2012, after a career that included practicing law and teaching math. Wisconsin’s win went to Democrat David Crowley , a Milwaukee County executive who beat Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany despite being significantly outspent. His path to the general election is a saga in itself: Crowley suspended his primary campaign before rejoining the race, with the backing of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, after the candidate he had been supporting dropped out. He ran as someone who can work across the aisle, and the result suggested Wisconsin voters believed him. Three more states elect their first women governors Three states that had never sent a woman to the governor’s office did so on Tuesday. In Tennessee, Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn won a race expected to favor her, though by a narrower margin than most anticipated. She focused on immigration, confronting China, and cutting spending, and will become the first woman ever to hold Tennessee’s governorship. In Minnesota, Democrat Amy Klobuchar defeated Republican Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House, and will become the state’s first woman governor when she takes office in January. Ohio produced the night’s biggest upset. Democrat Amy Acton , who served as the state’s chief public health officer during the pandemic, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race that turned notably rough in its final weeks, with an attack ad against Acton drawing national attention and criticism. She is now Ohio’s first woman governor, its first Jewish governor, and the first Democrat to hold the office in 20 years. What ten firsts in one night adds up to These results don’t necessarily add up to a single story about where the country is heading. Rather, what each of them does share is that the voters who elected them have done something that hadn’t been done before. Whether that came from changing attitudes about representation, the particular strengths of individual candidates, or just the specific dynamics of this incredible moment in the history of the United States of America, an election night this concentrated in firsts is certainly one to be remembered. items.description: Ένα γουρουνάκι που σώθηκε από μια δυνητικά πολύ κακή μοίρα ζει τώρα την ιστορία του Μπέιμπ, αφού το πήρε μέσα από μια συμπονετική προγιαγιά που έχει ένα καταφύγιο ζώων στην Αγγλία. Η συνταξιούχος κτηνιατρική νοσοκόμα Carole Webb έσωσε τον μικροσκοπικό άνθρωπο, που ονομάστηκε Tom, αφού τον ανακάλυψαν στην άκρη του δρόμου τον Μάρτιο σε ηλικία μόλις 1 ημέρας. Είναι ασαφές…
items.descriptionOriginal: A piglet saved from a potentially much unkinder fate is now living out the story of Babe after being taken in by a compassionate great-grandmother who owns an animal sanctuary in England. Retired veterinary nurse Carole Webb rescued the tiny fellow, dubbed Tom, after he was discovered on the side of the road in March at just 1 day old. It’s unclear how he came to be there, but Webb theorized that a sow may have given birth while being transported, and the piglet fell from the trailer. The person who found him kept him safe overnight before handing him over to her. FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Tom, who was about the size of a kitten at the time, was hand-reared indoors with hot water bottles and heat pads. Six months later, he’s grown into a pampered pig roaming a three-acre field at the Farm Animal Rescue Sanctuary in Stratford-upon-Avon. “Tom is really just like a real-life Babe,” Webb, 82, told SWNS, adding: “He’s really friendly with the chickens, he’s got a lot of chicken and cat friends — really anything that goes in to see him is his friend.” She said he acts more like a pet dog now than a typical pig, following the farm’s humans around and even coming when he’s called by name. He also has his own stuffed animals, loves to play, and enjoys his treats. “He plays around you and loves being near you. He’s got a big fluffy toy pig, and what he likes to do is lay over it,” she noted. “He loves his belly rubs, too — he’s just the friendliest little pig you could meet.” FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Named after Lord of the Rings character Tom Bombadil , Tom now weighs around 330-450 pounds, a big jump from the tiny piglet that could once fit in the palm of Webb’s hand. “He’s a bit boisterous so we don’t mix him with the sheep, but he’s got the run of one of the field,” said Webb. She noted that the sanctuary is home to about 350 animals, including sheep, cats, chickens, and one other pig. “We also feed the pigeons that are free-flying, and we’ve got an aviary that we put them in until they’re well,” she added. “We’ve got quite a collection.” The sanctuary is currently raising money to buy new land so it can continue caring for its animals. Donate here. This article was originally written by Adam Dutton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. What started as an opportunity to explore a part of India he knew little about soon became a much bigger commitment. Alongside teaching, he took on responsibilities in teacher training, community engagement, school activities and working closely with parents. Life in this remote region comes with challenges that many city schools rarely face. Poor roads, landslides, unreliable electricity and limited network connectivity make everyday tasks difficult. Medical facilities and essential shops can be several hours away. Yet, the children inspire Ashqar with their curiosity, talent and eagerness to learn. Now, he hopes to bring smartboards to the school and create at least one properly equipped smart classroom, giving these children access to visual and interactive learning resources. items.descriptionOriginal: Once the Diwali lights come down and the decorations are packed away , what happens to all those beautiful marigold garlands and rose petals? More often than not, they end up in the bin. But what if those same flowers could make your home smell wonderful, help your garden grow, or even give your old clothes a fresh splash of colour? Environmental consultant Thankam Kumaran believes there is plenty we can do with flowers long after the celebrations are over. Through her Instagram page @useful_human_being , she shares simple, creative ways to reduce everyday waste and make more sustainable choices. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Thankam Kumaran (@useful_human_being) In one of her videos, she shares seven ways to give leftover Diwali flowers a second life, using things you may already have at home. Give your festive flowers a second life 1. Make fragrant potpourri Collect the leftover flowers and place them in a small breathable bag. Add a few drops of essential oil and some camphor. Hang the bag in a room to release a pleasant fragrance and keep the space smelling fresh. 2. Prepare bio-enzymes Use the leftover flowers to make bio-enzymes through fermentation. This gives discarded floral waste another purpose instead of sending it to the bin. 3. Make incense sticks Dried flowers can be repurposed to make homemade incense sticks, allowing you to put the petals to use even after the celebrations. 4. Dye fabrics naturally Flower petals can also be used to extract natural colours and experiment with dyeing clothes and other fabrics. 5. Make homemade shampoo Certain flowers can be used to prepare homemade shampoo, offering another way to make use of what would otherwise be discarded. Environmental consultant Thankam Kumaran shares seven ways to reuse puja flowers. Photograph: (Orissa POST) 6. Turn them into compost Add leftover flowers to your compost pile. As they break down, they contribute organic matter that can help nourish the soil in your garden. 7. Use them as mulch Dried flowers can be spread around the base of plants as mulch. This helps cover the soil and retain moisture while making use of festive leftovers. Instead of treating flowers as waste once Diwali is over, these ideas provide easy ways to extend their usefulness. Whether you turn them into something fragrant for your home or use them to nourish your garden, a little effort can keep festive flowers from going to waste.

items.title: Τέσσερις άνδρες, τέσσερις χώρες, ένας κανόνας
items.titleOriginal: Four Men, Four Countries, One Rule
items.description: Σε μια κηδεία ενός ανθρώπου που δεν είπε ποτέ σε κανέναν ότι ήταν δυστυχισμένος, οι φίλοι που επέζησαν κάθισαν γύρω από ένα τραπέζι και μίλησαν για παιχνίδια στον υπολογιστή. Αυτή η λεπτομέρεια -- ακριβής και επώδυνη -- είναι το σημείο όπου ξεκινά αυτό το δοκίμιο και θέτει όλα όσα ακολουθούν. Ο συγγραφέας Rajeev Balasubramanyam παρακολούθησε τη θλίψη στο δωμάτιο να θάβεται υπό απόσπαση της προσοχής και αποφάσισε κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: At a funeral for a man who never told anyone he was unhappy, the surviving friends sat around a table and talked about computer games. That detail -- precise and painful -- is where this essay begins, and it sets up everything that follows. Writer Rajeev Balasubramanyam watched the grief in the room get buried under distraction and decided something had to change. He called three old friends scattered across Vancouver, London, Brussels, and Berlin, and he proposed the thing none of them had ever done: a men's circle. The rules were simple -- take turns speaking while others listen and no advice-giving. That last rule proved harder than it sounds; as he notes, dispensing solutions is simply "the way that we, as men, were used to talking." What emerged instead was something quieter and more rare: the feeling of being held. Over a year of online circles, a father died, a cancer survivor admitted he wasn't as fine as he'd thought, and a man in grief finally had space to feel it.

items.descriptionOriginal: At 75, Abdul Majeed Zargar still works with a craft that few people outside Kashmir's weaving workshops know exists. From his home in Amda Kadal Jogiwan, Srinagar, he hand-carves the wooden shuttle used to weave the region's celebrated Pashmina shawls. Known locally as the Mukh, the small tool carries the thread that makes every woven piece possible. Zargar is believed to be the last craftsman in Kashmir who makes these shuttles by hand. For nearly five decades, he has shaped wood into a tool that connects generations of weavers, even as the traditional skills behind Kashmir's textile heritage face declining demand. His story began with uncertainty. Before finding his calling, Zargar tried his hand at silver-making and knife-making. Neither trade worked for him, and he eventually turned to making Mukhs. Learning the craft took almost a year, during which he struggled to produce pieces that met the standards of experienced weavers. When he finally had a few shuttles ready to sell, he carried them from one workshop to another. Most people turned him away. He was close to abandoning the craft when a meeting in Khayam changed his life. Three shuttles that changed everything Zargar approached a sazvari, a trader who bought and sold weaving tools. The trader invited him upstairs, where experienced craftsmen were working. Nervous, Zargar showed them his handmade Mukhs. Having once struggled to find buyers for his work, Zargar now makes wooden shuttles that weavers value for their quality and durability. Photograph: ( Facebook/The Better India) They examined the pieces carefully and pointed out their flaws. Yet, before he left, they bought three pairs. The shuttles were not good enough for weaving, but the craftsmen wanted to encourage him to continue. When Zargar returned months later, he found the pieces still hanging on the wall. They had never been used. He asked why they had bought them if they were faulty. Their answer stayed with him: "If we had not bought them, you would have lost hope." The craftsmen also recommended him to other weavers and traders, helping him find customers who needed new shuttles or repairs. Slowly, his work improved, and his Mukhs became known for their quality and durability. There were times when weavers had to wait months for one of his handmade tools . That early encouragement became the foundation of a career spanning five decades. The tiny tool behind every Pashmina A Mukh may appear insignificant beside a finished shawl, but it performs one of the most important tasks in traditional weaving. The shuttle carries the weft yarn back and forth across the warp threads on a loom, allowing the fabric to take shape. With few young people willing to learn the craft, Zargar is turning to the next generation in his own family to keep the skill alive. Photograph: ( Facebook/Kashmir Life ) Without it, the loom cannot function. Every handwoven Pashmina or Tusha shawl depends on this simple movement before it can reach the stages of dyeing, embroidery and finishing. Zargar calls the Mukh the basis of Pashmina . Its importance lies not in its size or appearance, but in the work it enables. The tool connects the weaver to the larger ecosystem of Kashmiri textile artisans, whose skills transform delicate fibres into intricate fabrics. Over the years, Zargar has also improved the traditional design. Earlier, the metal components of the shuttle were made of iron, which could rust. He replaced them with brass, making the tool more durable and resistant to corrosion. Today, factory-made shuttle boats are cheaper and more readily available. But Zargar believes that the handmade Mukhs remain superior in quality and longevity. His tools are carved entirely by hand using chisels and files, without modern machinery. Passing down a dying craft The challenge facing Zargar is not simply the availability of tools, but the shrinking demand for traditional handloom weaving itself. As power looms replace handlooms and younger people move towards other professions, the need for handmade shuttles has declined. For Zargar, making Mukhs is about more than earning a livelihood. It is about preserving a small but essential part of Kashmir's Pashmina-making tradition. Photograph: ( Facebook/Daily Excelsior ) Zargar has tried to teach others, but finding willing apprentices has been difficult. Many young people prefer computer-based jobs or work in cities, leaving fewer people interested in learning a specialised craft that requires patience and years of practice. Despite decades of recognition and support from the Department of Handicrafts, he worries that awards alone cannot preserve the skill. What matters, he said, is that the craft continues. He is now teaching his son, hoping the knowledge will survive beyond his own lifetime. The work remains painstaking, and the future uncertain, but Zargar continues to carve the wooden tools that weavers depend on. "I do not know what will happen after me," he told Kashmir Life. "But as long as I can hold my tools, I will keep making them." For Kashmir's Pashmina, the survival of a centuries-old weaving tradition may depend on a small wooden shuttle, and on whether someone is willing to learn how to make it. Sources ' Kashmir's Last Shuttle ': by Afreen Ashraf for Kashmir Life, Published on 10 July, 2026, ' Meet Abdul Majeed Zargar: Kashmir's Last Surviving 'Mukh ' Craftsman': by Jahangeer Ganaie for Kashmir News Observer, Published on 19 May, 2025 ' For Want of a Tool, Kashmir's Famed Pashmina Industry Is Crumbling ': for Moneycontrol, Published in 2021

items.title: Από 27 ραπτομηχανές έως εργασίες στο εργοστάσιο, πώς οι γυναίκες Warli του Aarey ράβουν νέες αρχές
items.titleOriginal: From 27 Sewing Machines to Factory Jobs, How Aarey’s Warli Women Are Stitching New Beginnings
items.description: Καθώς πηγαίνω στο δάσος Aarey της Βομβάης (ο τελευταίος πράσινος πνεύμονας της πόλης), παίρνω τον υπόγειο διάδρομο του μετρό Aqua Line. Αλλά καθ' όλη τη διάρκεια της διαδρομής μου, δεν μπορώ να αγνοήσω την ενοχλητική αίσθηση ότι αυτή η επιλογή μεταφοράς είναι σχεδόν ιεροσυλία, δεδομένου ότι η κατασκευή του προκάλεσε σάλο το 2019 όταν απείλησε να εκτοπίσει 27 κοινότητες Warli Adivasi.…
items.descriptionOriginal: While making my way to Mumbai's Aarey Forest (the city's last green lung), I take the Aqua Line underground metro corridor. But throughout my ride, I can't ignore the nagging feeling that this choice of transport is almost sacrilege, given that its construction sparked an uproar in 2019 when it threatened to displace 27 Warli Adivasi communities that have called the forest home since the 1950s. But the metro is what will get me to my destination in the quickest time, and so I ignore the nagging guilt. In 2019, many of my trips were to the same forest to document the protests (as a journalism student); today, the purpose of my trip is different. The years have witnessed the community women being empowered through a stitching programme that has "changed their lives", according to many of their accounts. What began as an informal way of channelling their skills into a purpose has now solidified into formal jobs in factories across Mumbai. Their stories echo the resilience of a community that has repeatedly had to adapt to a city growing around it. Their stories echo the resilience of a community that has repeatedly had to adapt to a city growing around it. The same women whose homes and livelihoods once stood at the centre of a battle over Aarey's future are now finding new ways to assert their place within Mumbai's economic landscape. Through sewing, they have transformed a skill passed down within the community into a source of income, confidence and independence. What began as a small stitching initiative has, for some, become a pathway to formal employment. A conversation among the trees It's a Sunday morning when I plan my visit to the forest. While I was told that the women who work through the week would be at home (Sunday is their weekly off from the factory), the hamlets seem quiet. Surekha Burkhud (40), who lives in Khambachapada and has stayed back, shares that the factory had a sudden urgent requirement for a bulk order, and so the women were called. But she is quick to add, "The women don't mind going because they are paid OT (overtime). This is double their usual day's pay." It's just Surekha and me and the trees for company: chickoo, guava, jamun and ber (Indian jujube) . Drawing on context from them, she starts by emphasising the community's love for the trees in Aarey. "These were planted by some of the oldest members. When the metro was being built, we were so disturbed by the fact that our trees would get destroyed. They are our life," she shares. According to reports, hours after the Bombay High Court (HC) dismissed several petitions of the locals seeking Aarey to be declared a protected area, on 4 October 2019, opposing the construction of a 33-hectare metro car-shed in the forest, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) felled approximately 2,700 trees over the course of two days. Several protestors were detained, beaten up, and 29 were arrested on serious charges under Section 353, Section 332, Section 143 and Section 149. Seeing it pained the community members. I ask Surekha whether she's travelled by metro, given their aversion to its construction. She admits she has. "I was scared of being underground for so long," she sheepishly acknowledges. While admittedly the Aqua Line 3 has eased public commute for Mumbai's residents — reports had pegged the metro to eventually carry around 1.7 million passengers every day and bring down the number of vehicles on the road by up to 650,000 — Surekha says they find it inconvenient to access the metro as the car shed is built close to the hamlets, but the actual boarding gate is near Seepz. A PARI report had documented the plight of other Warli Adivasi families that weren't as fortunate as hers. Locals estimate that 70 Adivasi families lost their homes to the metro project. From 27, the number of padas is now down to 15. In addition to this, a common complaint they have is that because of the car shed area, water collects during the rains, causing flooding. That being said, the community is happy that for "the time being" their hamlet is safe. "But we never know," Surekha shrugs. A PARI report had documented the plight of other Warli Adivasi families that weren't as fortunate as hers . Locals estimate that 70 Adivasi families lost their homes to the metro project. From 27, the number of padas is now down to 15. But the community is resilient. And this same quality has helped them become empowered entrepreneurs. While forest produce was once their means of sustenance, tree felling in 2019 made them realise they needed to divert their attention to other income streams. They needed to recalibrate their lives. Weaving a story of change For Geeta Page (32), hope equates to a sewing machine. Her mud home in Khambachapada has a single bulb, whose light doesn't reach her work spot. Despite the fact that it is 11 am when these interviews are being conducted, Geeta's home gives the semblance of late evening. Her eyes bear the brunt of her determination, as she sews in the dimness of the room. "We stitch when we get orders. It takes five days to make a quilt, and we get Rs 400 per quilt. A bag takes less time to stitch," she shares. Geeta, like many other women, isn't solely reliant on the factory job, which, she says, is subject to the whims of the bosses. She also gets orders from Cassandra Nazareth and her team, who have been working in the region since 2016, attempting to help the women of these communities in any way they can. Cassandra is joined by Mahesh Bariya, Blasia Pinto and Rita Newnes. Each of them was drawn to join the effort after they recognised what Cassandra was trying to do. Mahesh shares, "When we first entered these villages, we realised that the women were not allowed to go out of the house. They weren't working. So, we started skill development programmes in three villages in 2015 to sell the products made by the women: tote bags, drawstring pouches, laddoos , modaks ." The impact left an imprint on their psyche. "Then slowly, we started giving the women cloth on which they could paint Warli art, and these would be given outside for stitching into bags. That's when we came up with the idea that, instead of outsourcing the stitching, why don't we let the women themselves stitch and earn?" Mahesh adds. Of course, formalising the products for sale would require proper training. "So we gave them 27 machines. After the lockdown, they were approached by factories. It gives them a livelihood," he adds. Surekha, who has completed four years at the factory in Andheri's MIDC, says she likes the work. For many of the women, it was more a question of continuing what they knew. "I had learnt stitching in my mother's house before getting married," Surekha says. "It was nice to continue it through the job role." PF and medical cards Having a bank account and actually using it are two very different things. According to reports, in India, one in three bank accounts belongs to a woman, but women only hold about a fifth of the total money deposited in banks. Even when women possess banking skills, structural barriers leave them unable to utilise their deposits or access credit. But through this factory work, a different story is unfolding in Aarey Forest's hamlets. Take Renuka (28), for instance. "I stitch at the factory in MIDC. We also get medical cards. Every month, some amount (Rs 190) gets deducted from our salary, and we can avail of all facilities if required," she shares. Renuka's daughter and husband are also covered by the card. Prior to the factory job, she wasn't working. Now, Renuka feels empowered. Her story echoes many other women's too. For instance, Shubhangi Rohakar (35). Shubhangi looks forward to the Rs 15000 payment that lands in her account every month. She explains that, while her salary is Rs 20,000 at the factory, Rs 1800 goes towards the PF (Provident Fund, which is a retirement savings scheme), Rs 190 for the medical card and Rs 3000 for a loan that she has taken for the new home that they are building. "It's the first time in my life that I am getting a PF," she smiles. Shubhangi explains that they even got help from "Kashi ma'am (Cassandra, as the women call her) in opening their bank accounts, where they could deposit the money. "They helped in opening zero-balance bank accounts. A lot of women did not have accounts, and we did not know how to save our money. We had never stepped out of the village," she shares. The women are grateful that the stitching programme led to all of this. She's also found the ESIC Card (medical card) extremely useful. "Last year I had a stomach problem and needed a sonography and blood tests," she shares. Everything was done free of cost, as well as consultation with the doctor. The women are grateful that the stitching programme led to all of this. While many of their husbands were sceptical of this empowerment, Mahesh says once they started seeing the money come in, they were on board. Changing their lives through projects While sitting in Surekha's home, I spot a drum set. Her son Jatin (23) tells me it was given to him by Cassandra. Rita explains that this is part of the 'Aur Chalao' project, through which they give pre-loved (a better way of saying second-hand) items donated by Mumbaikars to families in Aarey. The drum set was one of these. But Jatin needed to go for classes to learn how to play the drums. And this is where his mother's additional income came in. "It also helped a lot in the home with rations and our college books," he says. This wasn't the first time Surekha was earning. As part of the tribal lunch programme started by Cassandra and her team, Surekha and the women would cook using forest produce and host lunches in the padas . Blasia says it would often make her nostalgic about vacations in Goa. "It was so nice to see these women cooking on firewood, with their children hanging around. As the husbands began to see that it was bringing in income, they started taking care of the children," she explains. The funds that they raised through the lunches were used to refurbish the existing borewells." Any additional income is welcome, says Arti Kirkire (31), who says that she is using her income from her factory job to make their home. "The sewing machines given to us helped us learn how to stitch," she shares. Arti's daughter was an infant when she first took up the factory job. Being away from 9.30 am to 6.30 pm was tough. "But the people in the community used to watch her; my in-laws too would help," she says. Getting a paycheque, she says, is a boon. "Have you bought anything for yourself?" I ask. "Just for the house," she smiles. Considering the shift ends in the evening, I wonder how the women travel and if it's safe. They share that a bus picks them up and drops them back. They are glad about this option as it's tough to predict the forest's rhythm. In 2022, 10 animal attacks were reported in Aarey in a single year. Geeta once used to fear venturing into the forest to relieve herself at night. She would control her urge. Now, the 47 bio-toilets (in close quarters to every home and shared among a couple of families each) are a blessing, she says. These have limited the human-animal conflict when community members would venture to attend nature's call. The Nazareth Foundation has also crowd-funded and got 12 domestic flour mills for the women, which eases their previous 2.5 km walk and helped with building water tanks with a capacity of 5000 litres. And while the world around them changes, their inner worlds change too, with a stitching programme helping them form their own identities. Sources 'In Photos | Warli Adivasis Recall Birsa Munda in Fight to Save Aarey' by Sushmita, Published on 11 November 2019. 'Aarey protests: Supreme Court steps in to save Mumbai trees after protests' , Published by the BBC on 7 November 2019. 'Aarey Adivasis: 'Then we lost this land of ours' by Aayna, Published on 24 October 2019. 'Financial Inclusion of Women: Current Evidence from India' by Sunaina Kumar, Published on 17 August 2023. '10 animal attacks reported from Aarey and SGNP in one year; residents fear for their lives' by Pratip Acharya, Published on 6 November 2022.

items.title: Ισχυρότερο εμβόλιο γρίπης συνδέεται με σχεδόν 55% χαμηλότερο κίνδυνο εμφάνισης Αλτσχάιμερ
items.titleOriginal: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
items.description: Μια εκπληκτική νέα μελέτη δείχνει ότι ένα ισχυρότερο εμβόλιο γρίπης θα μπορούσε να προσφέρει στους ηλικιωμένους σημαντικά μεγαλύτερη προστασία έναντι της νόσου του Αλτσχάιμερ. Ερευνητές στο UTHealth Houston ανέλυσαν σχεδόν 200.000 ενήλικες ηλικίας 65 ετών και άνω και διαπίστωσαν ότι όσοι έλαβαν εμβόλιο υψηλής δόσης κατά της γρίπης είχαν σχεδόν 55% χαμηλότερο κίνδυνο να αναπτύξουν Αλτσχάιμερ.…
items.descriptionOriginal: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that those who received a high-dose influenza vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's, compared with a 40% reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.

items.title: 10 παραδόσεις ευεξίας από όλο τον κόσμο για να μπείτε στη ζωή σας
items.titleOriginal: 10 Wellness Traditions From Around the World to Weave Into Your Life
items.description: Η λέξη «ευεξία» μπορεί να δημιουργεί εικόνες από πολυτελείς περιποιήσεις σπα και πολυτελή καταφύγια, αλλά δεν χρειάζεται να κλείσετε μια πολυτελή απόδραση για να αυξήσετε τη ζωτικότητά σας – οι καθημερινές δραστηριότητες και οι μικρές, σκόπιμες συνήθειες μπορούν να είναι εξίσου αναζωογονητικές. Διαφορετικοί πολιτισμοί σε όλο τον κόσμο έχουν αναπτύξει εδώ και καιρό μοναδικές τεχνικές για την προώθηση της υγείας, της ευτυχίας και γενικότερα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The word “wellness” may conjure images of lavish spa treatments and high-end retreats, but you don’t have to book a luxury getaway to increase your vitality — everyday activities and small, intentional habits can be equally restorative. Different cultures around the world have long developed unique techniques to promote health, happiness, and overall well-being, from the Turkish concept of savoring idle pleasure to “forest bathing” in Japan. Join us as we explore 10 wellness traditions you can adopt to infuse more peace and balance into our often-overwhelming world. 1. Schemeren | The Netherlands antolikjan/iStock If you struggle to unwind after a long day, the Dutch concept of “dusking,” or “schemeren,” may be just what you’re looking for. The practice is remarkably effortless: Simply pull up a chair and pause for a while to watch the day turn into night. “Noticing twilight requires a persistent kind of attention. It’s like a shy, rare animal. You have to take your time. Stay focused,” author Marjolijn van Heemstra told the BBC , adding that it’s an important opportunity to reconnect with the world around us. “If you don’t know a tree, even if it’s in front of your house, because you never take the time to look at it, you don’t mind it being cut,” she said. “So, it’s about seeing things and trying to establish a relationship with them and then maybe caring for them.” 2. La Passeggiata | Italy Another evening ritual — la passeggiata — is a bit more active. In Italy, many people take an after-dinner stroll around town, which offers a way to connect with neighbors, reduce stress, and improve digestion, per the BBC . Although walking is widely recommended as an accessible and effective exercise , la passeggiata is more about relaxation and social bonds than fitness. 3. Hygge | Denmark Liudmila Chernetska/iStock Scandinavian winters tend to be long and dark, but the Danish tradition of hygge can make the season more enjoyable. Stemming from an Old Norse word meaning “protected from the outside world,” hygge centers on creating a cozy, comfortable environment, with an emphasis on self-care, relaxation, and spending time with loved ones. While it’s often associated with tangible things like warm drinks and soft blankets, it’s also a mindset focused on making small moments feel more meaningful. 4. Ubuntu | Southern Africa In certain sub-Saharan African cultures, including the Zulu and Xhosa, the philosophy and practice of ubuntu emphasize the importance of community and interconnectedness. Although it goes by many different names, ubuntu is apparent throughout societies across the continent, according to The Open University . At its core, it emphasizes the role individuals play in contributing to the greater good through intentional connection, mutual support, and a shared commitment to equality, equity, and fairness. In daily life, this can look like sharing resources and checking in on neighbors. As a whole, it’s about recognizing the humanity in everyone you meet. And the benefits may extend beyond your community: Research suggests that being kind to others can help your own well-being, too. 5. Sobremesa | Spain and Latin America JulieanneBirch/iStock Another custom grounded in community is “sobremesa,” which means “upon the table.” Popular in Spain and throughout Latin America, the centuries-old way of life involves lingering after a meal to relax, savor the moment, and chat — sometimes for hours. “It’s about an interchange of experiences, knowledge, and laughs. It encourages you to be present, not worrying about your troubles, and appreciate the simple moments in life,” Mexico City restaurateur Lorea Olavarri told Food & Wine . 6. Keyif | Turkey Turkey is famous for its hammam spas, but one of its perhaps lesser-known wellness traditions can be embraced anywhere. Keyif, “an ancient art of meaningful idleness,” is a state of mind focused on finding quiet joy in simple pleasures, per Eastern Turkey Tours . Unlike simply unwinding, keyif involves being fully present and savoring the more subdued moments, from sipping your first cup of coffee in the morning while watching the sun rise to gazing out the window and listening to the birds. 7. Dadirri | Australia Thurtell/iStock In Australia’s First Nations communities, the art of deep, intentional listening — often called dadirri — is an integral part of cultural preservation, community cohesion, and individual well-being. The ancient practice encourages people to connect with one another and the natural world, according to Aboriginal learning platform Creative Spirits . But it also extends beyond that to encompass self-reflection, contemplation, and an awareness of your origins, purpose, and place in the world. “It does wonders for a person to just be still and listen to someone else talk about their life and how they probably came through things,” late Aboriginal singer-songwriter Archie Roach once said about the importance of mindful listening, per the platform, adding: “You never know what you’ll learn.” 8. Shinrin-Yoku | Japan Ample research points to the mental and physical benefits of spending time in nature, and the Japanese tradition of shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, can help you reap them. Despite the name, there are no bathtubs involved, and even the forest is optional. All it takes is spending some time in a green space and using your senses to take it all in, whether at a botanical garden, city park, or lush woodland. Touch the soft moss, breathe in the fresh air, and listen to the birds as you gaze at the trees. “Forest therapy [can help us] see the truth that we are interconnected and interdependent. It offers us intentional time to be with ourselves, each other, and the natural world,” Regan Stacey, founder of The Forest Therapy School , told Vogue . 9. Friluftsliv | Norway Glenn Pettersen/iStock Meaning “open-air living,” this philosophy focuses on connecting with nature year-round, regardless of the weather. Popularized in the 1850s by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, friluftsliv remains a cultural mainstay throughout Scandinavia, according to the BBC . In fact, many employers in the region build outdoor recreation time into the workday. Although a Monday morning hike may not be realistic for everyone, we can all embrace friluftsliv by setting aside time to venture outside as often as we can. 10. Rhythmic Movement and Dance | Various African Cultures While not a singular tradition, dance is central to numerous cultures across the African continent and its diasporas . Although often ritualistic or ceremonial, moving one’s body rhythmically to music is also an integral part of everyday life that can foster both community and individual well-being. “Dancing is a full-body workout that benefits both the mind and body,” Liza Osagie-Clouard, orthopedic surgeon and founder of Solice Health in London, England, told British Vogue . “It improves cardiovascular health, increases flexibility, strengthens muscles, and enhances coordination,” she added. Moreover, listening to music — including the rhythmic drumming that often accompanies traditional dances — can stimulate the release of chemicals like dopamine and serotonin in the brain, helping to alleviate anxiety, enhance mood, and facilitate emotional release. items.descriptionOriginal: A Polish monk began each day with seven bows -- a gesture of apology toward a father he couldn't face. Bhikshu Jin Wei's story is not a tidy arc of spiritual progress; it's an honest account of how the hunger for transformation can become its own trap, and the gentle process of attuning to each moment. The turning came quietly, through a single word: a Thai Forest monk suggested a one-word loving-kindness mantra, and Jin Wei sat in the meditation hall asking himself what his word was. Immediately, it came: "safe". What followed was the discovery that the compassion he had been excavating through discipline had been waiting in his body all along -- "our body remembers our trauma," he reflects, "but the body also keeps the love." While on a trip back to Poland earlier this year, he experienced profound, full-circle moments along a softening journey: giving a talk at his own university and sitting down to a vegetarian lunch lovingly offered by his meat-eating family. The monastery, he suggests, is not only a physical place but a quality of listening, available to anyone willing to stop and ask what word is waiting to open their heart.

items.descriptionOriginal: Visitors to London’s British Museum can admire a remarkable example of Roman ingenuity that’s considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world. Dated to the fourth century, the ornate Lycurgus Cup is a soft jade green — or a striking ruby red, depending on where the light source is positioned. The goblet’s color-changing capability has long perplexed scientists. No one is sure exactly how it was created, but the consensus is that Romans added tiny bits of gold and silver to their glass mixture, forming layers of nanoparticles that interact with light differently depending on their size and shape. Experts had struggled to devise a reliable method of re-creating the material in quantity, but now, for the first time, the mystery appears to have been solved. Melding an ancient recipe with modern science, a glass specialist from the University of Sheffield has reproduced the effect, and commissioned a sculpture that pays homage to the original. Lisa Hollands, with the institution’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, took on the challenge, which was “very much a labor of love,” per a news release from the university. She worked with a Roman glass expert to develop a base that mimicked those used nearly two millennia ago, then set about experimenting with different furnace types, oxygen levels, and more. She said she knew it would be a much more complicated task than simply sprinkling some gold and silver nanoparticles into a mixture, but did think at one point, “If the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’” Finally, Hollands landed on a recipe for glass that looked opaque green under reflected light but red when a light was shone directly on it. “To me, it’s magic,” she told The Guardian . So how exactly does it work? “White light is made up of many different colors and you see this when there is a rainbow in the sky. Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of light and in certain conditions they block certain colors due to the light affecting the electrons in the atoms,” she explained to the outlet. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through. If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see,” she continued. Hollands and her project manager approached U.K. glass artist Elliot Walker, who won Season 2 of Netflix’s Blown Away , to create a finished piece that could be exhibited at Sheffield’s upcoming Festival of the Mind, which runs Nov. 6-15. It will then go on permanent display at the university’s Turner Museum of Glass . “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands,” Walker said in the release. The Lycurgus Cup depicts the legend of King Lycurgus from Homer’s Iliad , showing the triumph of the Greek god Dionysus over the lawgiver Lycurgus . The 2026 homage bridges the time between the Roman artwork and now. “I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass ,” said Walker. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture , with the globe replaced by a cup.” RELATED: Researchers Re-Create 5,000-Year-Old Egyptian Blue, the World’s Oldest Synthetic Pigment Once Lost to Science
